    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):
            metrics['input_range_ok'] = bool(
                mean_input_range_error <= STATLIMITS['input_range_error'])
    
        # match outputs based on range, fraction, and semantic similarity of names
        output_matches, output_match_costs = match_outputs(
            submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
        )
        metrics['output_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in output_matches
        ]
    
        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))
        metrics['output_match_mean_cost'] = mean_output_match_cost
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats['output_range']
        ref_output_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_output_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])

They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. It is in the file `/app/methodpaper.pdf`\n30\t  - A white paper about spike sorting and quality control is in the file `/app/ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`\n31\t- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n32\t- **Code**:\n33\t  - `/app/code` contains code from `/app/methodpaper.pdf`.\n34\t- **Data** from the papers are in the directory `/app/data`.\n35\t- **Documentation** on the **NWB** file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io. Documentation about `pynwb` is at https://pynwb.readthedocs.io/en/stable/. `pynwb` documentation is also downloaded to `/app/pynwb_docs/`.\n36\t\n37\t## Decoder Task\n38\t\n39\t- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \n40\t- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\n41\t- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \n42\t\n43\t### Decoder Inputs:\n44\t- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n45\t- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\n46\t\n47\t### Decoder Outputs\n48\t- Lick direction **choice** (left, right, no lick, per-trial)\n49\t- **Outcome** (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\n50\t- **Early lick** (no, yes, per-trial)\n51\t- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\n52\t  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\n53\t  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n54\t  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n55\t  - 3: not visible\n56\t\n57\t## Target Data Format\n58\t\n59\t- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n60\t- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n61\t\n62\t```python\n63\tdata = {\n64\t    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n65\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n66\t            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n67\t            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n68\t            ...\n69\t        ],\n70\t        [  # list of trials for session 2\n71\t            ...\n72\t        ],\n73\t        ...\n74\t    ],\n75\t\n76\t    'input': [  # list of sessions\n77\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n78\t            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n79\t            ...\n80\t        ],\n81\t        ...\n82\t    ],\n83\t\n84\t    'output': [  # list of sessions\n85\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n86\t            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n87\t            ...\n88\t        ],\n89\t        ...\n90\t    ],\n91\t\n92\t    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n93\t    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n94\t\n95\t    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n96\t    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n97\t        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n98\t    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n99\t\n100\t    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n101\t    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n102\t    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n103\t        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n104\t        ...\n105\t    ],\n106\t\n107\t    'metadata': {\n108\t        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n109\t        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n110\t        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n111\t        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n112\t        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n113\t        ...\n114\t    }\n115\t}\n116\t```\n117\t\n118\t### Key Format Requirements\n119\t\n120\t- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n121\t  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n122\t  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n123\t  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n124\t\n125\t- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n126\t  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n127\t  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n128\t    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n129\t    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n130\t    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n131\t  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n132\t  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n133\t  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n134\t\n135\t- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n136\t  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n137\t  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n138\t  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n139\t  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n140\t  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n141\t\n142\t- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n143\t- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n144\t  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n145\t\n146\t- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n147\t- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n148\t\n149\t- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n150\t  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n151\t\n152\t- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n153\t  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n154\t- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n155\t  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n156\t\n157\t- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n158\t  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n159\t  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n160\t  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n161\t  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n162\t  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n163\t\n164\t## Python environment\n165\t\n166\t- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n167\t- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n168\t- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n169\t\n170\t## Decoder Reference\n171\t\n172\t- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n173\t- Optional arguments:\n174\t  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n175\t  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n176\t  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n177\t- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n178\t\n179\t### Purpose\n180\t\n181\tThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n182\t1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n183\t2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n184\t3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n185\t4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n186\t5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n187\t\n188\t### Consistency requirements\n189\t\n190\tYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n191\t- Loading of data\n192\t- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n193\t- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n194\t- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n195\t\n196\tTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n197\t\n198\tWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n199\t\n200\tDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n201\t\n202\tCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n203\t\n204\tYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference papers and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n205\t\n206\t---\n207\t\n208\t## Conversion Workflow\n209\t\n210\t**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference papers and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n\n---\n\n## Conversion Workflow\n\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. Each step has explicit completion criteria. Do not proceed to the next step until the current step is complete. Use the exact step names below when documenting progress in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n\n**STATUS TRACKING**: At the start of each step, update its status to `IN PROGRESS` in CONVERSION_NOTES.md. When complete, update to `COMPLETE`. This helps you and the user track progress.\n\n---\n\n### Step 0: Setup and Initialization\n\n**Goal**: Set up the working environment and create the notes file.\n\n**Actions**:\n1. **FIRST**: Create `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` with the template structure shown at the end of this document\n2. Variables important to experiments\n  - Temporal alignment\n  - Temporal binning\n- Read the reference papers to find information about expected decoder accuracy.\n\n**Done when**: You have documented expected dataset statistics and processing details in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 3\".\n\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 4, update Step 3 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n\n---\n\n### Step 4: Check for Consistency\n\n**Goal**: Verify your understanding is consistent across all sources. \n\n**Actions**:\n- Compare your understanding of:\n  - Save plots as `processing_<session_id>.png`.\n- Reuse code from reference code bases where appropriate\n- Use `pynwb` to interface with the data. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\n  a. Verify the sample data structure matches the specification.\n  b. Check dimensions are consistent across trials/sessions.\n  c. Check that no data is missed during conversion. \n  d. Validate that metadata accurately describes the data.\n2. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \n5. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_full_out.txt`. \n6. Check that no data was lost during conversion \n7. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\n8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `/app/verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\n9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\n\n**Done when**:\n- `/app/converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\n- `/app/verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\n- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\n- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 9\"\n\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `/app/converted_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\n\n---\n\n### Step 10: Critical Review 1\n\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Check that your code robustly handles issues in the original data. \n\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n2. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n\nWrite a report to CONVERSION_NOTES.md describing **every** check you did, to help convince the user that the conversion code works. **Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 10\".\n\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 11 until you have checked for consistency between **every** statistic in the reference texts, code, and data and documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Step 10. \n\n---\n\n### Step 11: Full Decoder Training\n\n**Goal**: Validate the decoder on the **complete** dataset.\n\n**⚠️ IMPORTANT**: This step must complete fully. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the papers. \n\n**Done when**: \n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 11\" with a table of accuracies\n\n---\n\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\n\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\n\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \n\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers**\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference papers\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the papers' accuracy for each variable\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \n\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n\n---\n\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n\n**Actions**:\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n  - Key decisions and rationale\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n  - Validation results and tables\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\n  - Dataset description\n  - How to load and use the converted data\n  - Output format specification\n  - Key statistics\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n\n---\n\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. Use `pynwb` to load data files.\n2. Match the target data structure exactly\n3. Preserve all relevant information from the source\n4. Have consistent dimensions across trials/sessions\n5. Match information provided in the reference texts\n6. Include complete and accurate metadata\n7. Be reproducible with documented code\n8. All required files must be created:\n  - `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`\n  - `/app/convert_data.py`\n  - `/app/converted_data.pkl`\n  - `/app/sample_data.pkl`\n  - `/app/README.md`\n  - `/app/train_decoder_full_out.txt`\n  - `/app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\n  - `/app/verification_sample_out.txt`\n  - `/app/train_decoder_sample_out.txt`\n  - `/app/conversion_full_out.txt`\n  - `/app/verification_full_out.txt`\n9. **Pass all validation checks**:\n  - Data summary shows correct structure\n  - Visual inspection reveals no artifacts\n  - Dataset size and distribution statistics match reference texts\n  - Decoder achieves good accuracy\n  - Any validation failures are investigated and resolved\n10. Include comprehensive CONVERSION_NOTES.md documenting all decisions and validation results\n11. Where nothing was recorded, the session or trial is excluded, since emitting it would fabricate data — a trial with no spikes would otherwise appear as 4 s of 0 Hz across every unit.         }\n462\t        return result\n463\t\n464\t\n465\t# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n466\t# Diagnostic plots\n467\t# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n611\tdef _worker(args):\n612\t    path, collect_debug = args\n613\t    try:\n614\t        return convert_session(path, collect_debug=collect_debug)\n615\t    except Exception as exc:  # keep one bad file from killing the whole run\n616\t        import traceback\n617\t        traceback.print_exc()\n618\t        return {'identifier': os.path.basename(path), 'path': path,\n619\t                'rejected': f'exception: {exc!r}'}\n620\t\n621\t\n622\tdef main():\n623\t parser.add_argument('--show-processing', action='store_true',\n632\t                        help='save processing_<session>.png for up to 2 sessions')\n633\t    parser.add_argument('--workers', type=int,\n634\t                        default=min(24, os.cpu_count() or 1))\n635\t    args = parser.parse_args()\n636\t\n637\t    t_start = time.time()\n638\t    files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n639\t    print(f'found {len(files)} NWB files in {DATA_DIR}')\n640\t\n641\t    if args.sample:\n642\t        # Curation is cheap compared with conversion, but not free; in sample mode just\n643\t        # walk the list until 2 sessions have been converted.\n644\t        files = files[:8]\n645\t        print(f'--sample: trying the first len(jobs) > 1:\n654\t        with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=args.workers) as pool:\n655\t            for res in pool.map(_worker, jobs):\n656\t                results.append(res)\n657\t                _report(res)\n658\t    else:\n659\t        for job in jobs:\n660\t            res = _worker(job)\n661\t            results.append(res)\n662\t            _report(res)\n663\t\n664\t    kept = [r for r in results if r.get('rejected') is None]\n665\t    rejected = [r for r in results if r.get('rejected') is not None]\n666\t    if args.sample:\n667\t        kept = kept[:2]\n668\t\n669\t    print(f'\\ncurated {len(kept)} sessions, rejected {len(rejected)}')\n670\t    for r in rejected:\n671\t        print(f'  REJECTED {r[\"identifier\"]}: {r[\"rejected\"]}')\n672\t\n673\t    if protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)\n682\t    size = os.path.getsize(args.outfile)\n683\t    print(f'wrote {size / 1e9:.2f} GB in {time.time() - t_write:.1f} s')\n684\t    print(f'total elapsed {time.time() - t_start:.1f} s')\n685\t    summarise(data, kept)\n686\t\n687\t\n688\tdef _report(res):\n689\t    if res.get('rejected') is not None:\n690\t        print(f'  - {res[\"identifier\"]}: ({res[\"elapsed\"]:.1f}s)')\n694\t    sys.stdout.flush()\n695\t\n696\t\n697\tdef assemble(sessions):\n698\t    \"\"\"Build the final dictionary from the per-session results.\"\"\"\n699\t    sessions = 'subjects': mice,\n704\t        'subject_idx': np.array([mice.index(r['mouse']) for r in sessions], dtype=np.int64),\n705\t        'brain_regions': list(REGION_NAMES),\n706\t r['input'] = None\n720\t        data['output'].append([np.ascontiguousarray(x) for x in r['output']])\n721\t        r['output'] = None\n722\t\n723\t    data['metadata'] = {\n724\t        'dataset': A series of pure '\n728\t            'tones during the sample epoch (3 kHz instructs lick-right, 12 kHz instructs '\n729\t            'lick-left) is followed by a 1.2 s delay in which licking must be withheld, '\n730\t            'then an auditory go cue opens a 1.5 s answer epoch in which the mouse licks '\n731\t            'the left or right port; a correct lick is rewarded with water. Constant within a trial.',\n756\t            'early lick during the sample or delay epoch: 0 no, 1 yes. Constant within a trial.',\n757\t            'vertical position of the tongue in the side-view video, per 50 ms bin: 3 if the '\n758\t            'tongue is not visible (DeepLabCut likelihood <= '\n759\t            f'{TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD} in every frame of the bin), otherwise 0/1/2 for '\n760\t            'below the 40th percentile / between the 40th and 60th percentile / above the '\n761\t            '60th percentile of the visible per-bin y values of that session.',\n762\t        ],\n763\t        'neuron_curation': \"units['classification'] == 'good' (per-region quality-control \"\n764\t                           'classifier of Chen, Liu et al. 2023); all such units carry a CCF '\n765\t                           'annotation.',\n766\t        'trial_curation': 'trials outside the electrophysiological recording (units\\' '\n767\t                          'obs_intervals) removed; auto-water and free-water trials '\n768\t                          'removed (reference get_regular_trial_mask); trials without '\n769\t                          'video coverage of the analysis window removed.          'lick-left and lick-right control trials (data paper STAR '\n775\t                            'Methods), all evaluated on the trials that survive trial '\n776\t                            'curation, which also removes sessions whose video or ephys '\n777\t                            'covers too few trials.',\n778\t        'known_limitation': 'The NWB release stores spikes only within |\n156\t\n157\t### Processing Details\n158\t- **Temporal alignment**: everything is aligned to the **go cue**. The reference `.mat` export stores\n159\t  spike times already relative to the go cue; markers are aligned with\n160\t  `times_for_frames = arange(n_frames)*0.0034 − go_time` (go-cue-relative), over `[-3, 1.5)` s.\n161\t- **Temporal binning**: reference uses 40 ms width / 3.4 ms stride sliding bins → firing **rate**\n162\t  (spikes / bin_width). The present task instead prescribes **50 ms bins**, so I use\n163\t  non-overlapping 50 ms bins over `[-2.5, +1.5)` s (80 bins), rate = count / 0.05 s.\n164\t- **Marker handling** (method paper Methods): outliers found with a 5-sigma velocity threshold and\n165\t  imputed from neighbouring frames; \"when the tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth … we set\n166\t  the tongue position to its mean value\". Here occlusion is an explicit output category instead.\n167\t\n168\t### Curation Steps\n169\t\n170\t**Neuron curation rules**:\n171\t1. Keep only units labelled `good` by the region-specific QC classifier\n172\t   (`units['classification'] == 'good'`); this is the reference's `qc_mode='classifier'` /\n173\t   `goodunits/*.mat` selection and the paper's 69,943-unit set.\n174\t2. see Step 5 \"Key Decisions\"\n182\tfor why early-lick / no-response / photostim trials must be **kept** for this decoding task.\n183\t\n184\t**Session curation**: performance > 65 % and ≥ 50 correct lick-left and ≥ 50 correct lick-right\n185\tcontrol trials (data paper), plus ≥ 1 good unit.\n186\t\n187\t### Decoders Trained (accuracies reported in the papers)\n188\t| Decoded variable | Reported accuracy |\n189\t|---|---|\n190\t| Choice, from **video** (embedding), before sample epoch | AUC 0.51 ± 0.06 (n = 106 sessions) |\n191\t| Choice, from **video**, sample+delay epoch | AUC 0.66 ± 0.12 |\n192\t| Choice, from **video**, 2nd half of response epoch | AUC 0.99 ± 0.01 |\n193\t| Choice, from video markers, response epoch | AUC 0.88 ± 0.01 |\n194\t| Choice, from single-neuron delay firing rate | threshold AUC > 0.65 used to call a neuron \"choice-modulated\" |\n195\tNeither paper reports a multi-class accuracy for choice/outcome/early-lick/tongue decoding from\n196\tpopulation neural activity, so there is no direct numerical target for this task's decoder; Trials, events, units and tracking are read through the\n   `pynwb`/`hdmf` API (`nwb.intervals['trials']`, `nwb.acquisition[...]`, `nwb.units`,\n   `nwb.electrodes`). No further metric thresholds:\n   the 15 quality metrics were already consumed by that classifier, so re-thresholding them would\n   double-filter.\n3. **Session curation**: ≥1 good unit, **and** the data paper's behavioural criteria (control,\n   non-early-lick performance > 65 %; ≥50 correct lick-left and ≥50 correct lick-right control\n   trials). Bin *b* spans `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))`;\n   the bin centre `-2.475 + 0.05b` is used for time-valued inputs.\n6. **Firing rate**, not spike count (reference `sliding_histogram(rate=True)`): count / 0.05 s.\n   Bins lying outside the trial's `[start_time, stop_time]` interval necessarily contain no spikes\n   and get rate 0; this is a property of the release (see Step 4), and `metadata` records it.\n7. **Tongue visibility threshold** `likelihood > 0.9`. The DeepLabCut likelihood is extremely\n   bimodal (87 % of frames < 1e-4, 11 % > 0.999); the visible fraction changes by < 0.5 % of frames\n   between thresholds of 0.01 and 0.999, so the choice is immaterial (verified in Step 10).\n   A bin counts as visible if **any** frame inside it is visible, because a tongue protrusion lasts\n   only ~50–100 ms and a majority rule would drop genuine short protrusions straddling a bin edge.\n8. **Percentiles for the tongue discretisation** are computed **per session** over the visible\n   per-bin y-values of all retained trials of that session — the population that is actually being\n   labelled — so classes 0/1/2 hold 40 %/20 %/40 % of the visible bins by construction.\n9. **Choice on error trials** is the *opposite* of the instruction (the mouse licked the wrong\n   port), and `no lick` on `ignore` trials. This is the standard reading of `outcome` in this task\n   and matches the reference's `correctness` semantics (1 correct / 0 error / −1 no response).\n10. **Inputs are exactly the two the task specifies**; the go cue is not added as an input because\n    it is at t = 0 in every trial by construction.\n11. **Brain regions**: 14 coarse groups derived from the per-unit CCF annotation (Step 4). Region\n    names carry no hemisphere; the hemisphere of every neuron (from CCF ML vs the reference's\n    5700 µm midline) is stored separately in `metadata['neuron_hemisphere']`.\n\n### Planned No\nsmoothing, normalisation or baseline subtraction.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef window_edges(go_times):\n    return go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]\n\n\ndef bin_spike_times(spike_times, edges_abs):\n    pos = np.searchsorted(spike_times, edges_abs.ravel()).reshape(edges_abs.shape)\n    return np.diff(pos, axis=1).astype(np.int32)\n```\n\n```python\ncounts = np.empty((n_good, n_trials, N_BINS), dtype=np.int32)\nfor i, unit in enumerate(raw['good_units']):\n    counts[i] = bin_spike_times(np.asarray(spike_index[int(unit)]), edges)\nneural = np.ascontiguousarray(\n    counts.transpose(1, 0, 2).astype(np.float32) / BIN_WIDTH)\n```\n\niii. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms, non-overlapping, 80 bins spanning [-2.5, +1.5) s relative to the go cue, identical for\nevery trial and every session. A trial can contain several sample onsets because an\nearly lick replays the sample epoch, so the tone of a trial is defined as the **last**\n`sample_start_times` at or before that trial's go cue. The code asserts that such a tone exists\nand that it lies inside the trial.\n\nii.\n```python\n'sample_start': np.asarray(events['sample_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64),\n```\n\n```python\n# Tone onset = last sample-epoch onset at or before the go cue.  Early licking\n# replays the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several onsets; the\n# most recent one is the tone the animal is acting on.\ntone_idx = np.searchsorted(raw['sample_start'], go, side='right') - 1\nassert np.all(tone_idx >= 0), f\"{raw['identifier']}: go cue before any tone\"\ntone = raw['sample_start'][tone_idx]\nassert np.all(tone >= raw['start_time'][trial_idx] - 1e-9), (\n    f\"{raw['identifier']}: tone onset outside its trial\")\n```\n\niii. Step 4: \"Replays produce extra sample/delay onsets. 'Tone onset' is therefore defined as the\n**last** `sample_start_times` at or before the trial's go cue (always inside the trial: 0\nviolations dataset-wide).\" Step 5 maps it to the reference's `task_sample_time`.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. Because the bins are laid out around the go cue, the value of bin *b* on trial *t* is simply the\nbin centre plus the go-cue-to-tone gap: `BIN_CENTERS[b] + (go[t] - tone[t])`. The result is a\ncontinuous, time-varying `float32` row; it is negative for bins before the tone. Observed range on\nthe full dataset is [-1.525, 11.894] s (the long tail comes from early-lick replays that push the\ntone far back from the go cue).\n\nii.\n```python\ntime_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n...\ninputs = np.stack([time_from_tone, photostim], axis=1)  # (n_trials, 2, 80)\n```\n\n```python\n'seconds elapsed since the onset of the instruction tone (the last sample-epoch '\n'onset at or before the go cue; negative before the tone). Continuous.',\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"input value at bin *b* = `bin_centre_b − (tone_onset − go)` (seconds\nsince the tone)\". Step 9 cross-checks the resulting range against the raw data: \"go − tone: median\n1.85 s, min 0.95, max 10.42\" and notes the converted range [-1.525, 11.894] s is consistent once\nbin centres (±2.475 s) are added. Step 10 Check 2 re-derives 25 random (trial, bin) values straight\nfrom the NWB with `np.allclose(atol=1e-4)`.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is computed on exactly the grid that defines the neural binning — the same 80 bin centres of\nthe same go-cue-anchored window — so bin *k* of the input covers the same interval as bin *k* of\nthe firing rates by construction. No interpolation or separate alignment step exists.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_WIDTH * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)       # (81,)\nBIN_CENTERS = 0.5 * (BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_EDGES[1:])            # (80,)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = window_edges(go)                                     # neural\ntime_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]) # input 0\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 5: \"Bin *b* spans `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))`; the bin centre\n`-2.475 + 0.05b` is used for time-valued inputs.\" The `--show-processing` figure (panel 4) was used\nto confirm the alignment visually: \"the ramp cross[es] zero exactly at the marked true tone onset\".\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Photostimulation* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times.timestamps` and\n`BehavioralEvents/photostim_stop_times.timestamps` — the absolute on/off times of each\nphotostimulation event. The trials-table column `photostim_onset` (a string, `'N/A'` when there was\nno stimulation) is read but used only for the control-trial definition in session curation and as a\ncross-check. The trials table `start_time` is used to assign each stim event to its trial.\n\nii.\n```python\n'photostim_onset_str': np.asarray(trials['photostim_onset'][:]),\n'photostim_start': np.asarray(events['photostim_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64),\n'photostim_stop': np.asarray(events['photostim_stop_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64),\n```\n\niii. Step 1: \"The reference's photostim variable is `[laser_power, stim_type, laser_on_time,\nlaser_off_time]`, with on/off times re-referenced to the go cue. The NWB equivalent is\n`BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times`/`photostim_stop_times` (absolute) plus the trials-table\ncolumns `photostim_onset`/`photostim_power`/`photostim_duration`.\" Step 4 verifies the two are\nconsistent: \"`len(photostim_start_times)` equals the number of trials with\n`photostim_onset != 'N/A'` and they map 1:1 to those trials **in all 174 sessions**\", which\njustifies using the event timestamps (which need no string parsing) as the source.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. A binary (0/1 `float32`) time series, one value per 50 ms bin: a bin is 1 if its half-open\ninterval **overlaps** any `[photostim_start, photostim_stop)` interval. Each stim event is first\nmapped to its trial via `searchsorted` on `start_time`, then to the row of the kept-trial array;\nevents belonging to dropped trials are discarded. Trials and sessions with no stimulation come out\nall-zero.\n\nii.\n```python\nphotostim = np.zeros((n_trials, N_BINS), dtype=np.float32)\nif len(raw['photostim_start']):\n    # A bin [t0, t1) is \"on\" if it intersects any [stim_start, stim_stop).\n    stim_trial = np.searchsorted(raw['start_time'], raw['photostim_start'],\n                                 side='right') - 1\n    position = np.searchsorted(trial_idx, stim_trial)\n    in_kept = (position < n_trials) & (trial_idx[np.clip(position, 0, n_trials - 1)]\n                                       == stim_trial)\n    for row, on, off in zip(position[in_kept], raw['photostim_start'][in_kept],\n                            raw['photostim_stop'][in_kept]):\n        overlap = (edges[row, :-1] < off) & (edges[row, 1:] > on)\n        photostim[row, overlap] = 1.0\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"1 if the bin `[t0,t1)` intersects `[stim_start, stim_stop)`, else 0\",\nmapped to the reference's `task_stimulation[:,2:]`. The task specification requires\n\"Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\", so a per-trial\nflag was rejected in favour of a binary time series. Step 10 Check 5 covers the boundary case:\n\"Photostim offset 1 ms *after* the go cue (34.6 % of stim events) — kept as-is; it affects the\nsingle bin [0, 50 ms) and reflects the real stimulus\", and Step 4 confirms the timing against the\npaper's \"always ended before the Go cue\".\n\n## 4-c. How is the `input` *Photostimulation* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Via the same absolute bin-edge array used for the spikes: `edges` is `go[:, None] +\nBIN_EDGES[None, :]`, and the stim on/off times are absolute session times, so they are compared\nagainst those edges directly. No re-referencing or interpolation is done beyond mapping the event\nto its trial row.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = window_edges(go)               # same array used to bin the spikes\n...\noverlap = (edges[row, :-1] < off) & (edges[row, 1:] > on)\nphotostim[row, overlap] = 1.0\n```\n\niii. Everything in the NWB file is on one session-absolute clock (Step 4), so using the same\n`edges` array guarantees bin-for-bin correspondence with the firing rates. Verified in Step 10\nCheck 2 (\"**input 1**, 100 random (trial, bin) cells — overlap of the bin with any\n`[photostim_start, photostim_stop)` — PASS\") and visually in panel 1/4 of the processing figures,\nwhere the shaded photostim window in the spike raster coincides with the square wave in the input.\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction choice* derived from?\n\ni. The trials table has no choice column, so choice is derived from two columns:\n`trials['trial_instruction']` (`'left'` / `'right'`) and `trials['outcome']`\n(`'hit'` / `'miss'` / `'ignore'`).\n\nii.\n```python\n'instruction': np.asarray(trials['trial_instruction'][:]),\n'outcome': np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:]),\n...\ninstruction = raw['instruction'][trial_idx]\noutcome = raw['outcome'][trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"`trials['trial_instruction']` + `trials['outcome']` →\n`output[0]` = `lick_direction_choice`\", mapped to the reference's `trial_type` × `correctness`\n(`create_4fold_trial_type_mask`). Key Decision 9: \"This is the standard reading of `outcome` in\nthis task and matches the reference's `correctness` semantics (1 correct / 0 error / −1 no\nresponse).\"\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction choice*?\n\ni. Start from the instructed side (`left` → 0, `right` → 1); on a `miss` (error) trial flip it,\nbecause the mouse licked the opposite port; on an `ignore` trial set it to 2 (`no lick`). The\nresult is one integer per trial, written into row 0 of the `(n_trials, 4, 80)` `int8` output array\nand repeated across all 80 bins so that all four outputs share one time-varying array.\n`output_values[0] = ['left', 'right', 'no lick']`. Full-dataset distribution: left 0.447,\nright 0.443, no lick 0.109.\n\nii.\n```python\nCHOICE_LEFT, CHOICE_RIGHT, CHOICE_NOLICK = 0, 1, 2\n...\nchoice = np.where(instruction == 'left', CHOICE_LEFT, CHOICE_RIGHT)\n# An error trial means the mouse licked the port opposite the instruction.\nchoice = np.where(outcome == 'miss', 1 - choice, choice)\nchoice = np.where(outcome == 'ignore', CHOICE_NOLICK, choice)\n...\noutputs = np.empty((n_trials, 4, N_BINS), dtype=np.int8)\noutputs[:, 0, :] = choice[:, None]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 9: \"**Choice on error trials** is the *opposite* of the instruction (the\nmouse licked the wrong port), and `no lick` on `ignore` trials.\" Step 10 Check 2 verifies the\nderivation for every trial of 6 random sessions directly from the NWB, and includes the global\nconsistency check \"choice 'no lick' ⇔ outcome 'ignore' — PASS\".\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?\n\ni. Directly from `trials['outcome']`, which already holds exactly the three strings `'ignore'`,\n`'miss'` and `'hit'`.\n\nii.\n```python\n'outcome': np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:]),\n...\noutcome = raw['outcome'][trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 2 records that `outcome ∈ {hit, miss, ignore}` in the trials table and Step 5 maps it\none-to-one onto the requested output categories; no derivation is needed. The reference analogue is\n`behavior_report` / `correctness` (1 / 0 / −1).\n\n## 6-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?\n\ni. The three strings are mapped through a fixed dictionary to `0` ignore, `1` miss, `2` hit — the\norder given in the task specification — and written into row 1 of the output array, repeated across\nall 80 bins. `output_values[1] = ['ignore', 'miss', 'hit']`. Full-dataset distribution: ignore\n0.109, miss 0.153, hit 0.737.\n\nii.\n```python\nOUTCOME_CODE = {'ignore': 0, 'miss': 1, 'hit': 2}\n...\noutcome_code = np.array([OUTCOME_CODE[o] for o in outcome], dtype=np.int8)\noutputs[:, 1, :] = outcome_code[:, None]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"`trials['outcome']` → `output[1]` = `outcome`; `ignore`→0, `miss`→1,\n`hit`→2\", i.e. the code order of the instructions' \"Outcome (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\". It is\na per-trial label, so it is broadcast across bins like the other per-trial outputs.\n\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Early lick* derived from?\n\ni. Directly from `trials['early_lick']`, which holds `'early'` / `'no early'`.\n\nii.\n```python\n'early_lick': np.asarray(trials['early_lick'][:]),\n...\nearly = raw['early_lick'][trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 2/Step 5: the trials table flags early licking explicitly, so no derivation is needed;\nthe reference analogue is `behavior_early_report`.\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Early lick*?\n\ni. A boolean comparison to `'early'`, cast to `int8` (0 no, 1 yes), written into row 2 of the\noutput array and repeated across all 80 bins. `output_values[2] = ['no', 'yes']`. Full-dataset\ndistribution: no 0.885, yes 0.115 — matching the 0.114 early-lick fraction measured directly on\nthe raw trials tables.\n\nii.\n```python\nearly_code = (early == 'early').astype(np.int8)\n...\noutputs[:, 2, :] = early_code[:, None]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"`trials['early_lick']` → `output[2]`; `no early`→0, `early`→1\". The\nearly lick itself occurs during the sample or delay epoch, i.e. inside the -2.5 s window, but the\nflag is stored per trial, so it is broadcast across bins.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue y-position* derived from?\n\ni. `nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']`, whose\n`data` is `(n_frames, 3)` = (tongue x, tongue y, DeepLabCut likelihood) with matching per-frame\n`timestamps` (dt = 0.0034 s, ≈294 Hz). Column 1 is the y value, column 2 decides visibility; column\n0 is read but unused. The series is present in all 174 sessions.\n\nii.\n```python\ntongue = tracking['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\nout['video_t'] = np.asarray(tongue.timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64)\ntongue_data = np.asarray(tongue.data[:], dtype=np.float64)\nout['tongue_y'] = tongue_data[:, 1]\nout['tongue_likelihood'] = tongue_data[:, 2]\n```\n\niii. Step 2: \"`nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries']` — DeepLabCut tracking, `(n_frames, 3)` =\n`(x, y, likelihood)` with per-frame `timestamps`: `Camera0_side_JawTracking`,\n`Camera0_side_NoseTracking`, `Camera0_side_TongueTracking` (present in **all 174** sessions)\". Step\n5 maps it to the reference's `align_markers_between_lims` / `tongue_y` marker.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Three steps. (1) A frame counts as **visible** if its DeepLabCut likelihood > 0.9. (2) For each\n(trial, bin), the number of visible frames and the sum of their y values are obtained with prefix\nsums over the whole session indexed by the bin edges, giving the per-bin mean y of the *visible*\nframes only; bins with no visible frame get NaN. (3) Those per-bin means are discretised (see 8-c).\nA bin is treated as visible if **any** frame in it is visible.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD = 0.9\n...\ndef segment_sums(values, mask, edges_abs, sample_times):\n    pos = np.searchsorted(sample_times, edges_abs.ravel()).reshape(edges_abs.shape)\n    cum_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(mask)])\n    cum_v = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(np.where(mask, values, 0.0))])\n    n_frames_bin = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n    n_masked_bin = cum_n[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_n[pos[:, :-1]]\n    masked_sum = cum_v[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_v[pos[:, :-1]]\n    return n_frames_bin, n_masked_bin, masked_sum\n```\n\n```python\nvisible = raw['tongue_likelihood'] > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD\n_, n_visible_bin, y_sum_bin = segment_sums(\n    raw['tongue_y'], visible, edges, raw['video_t'])\nbin_visible = n_visible_bin > 0\ny_mean = np.where(bin_visible, y_sum_bin / np.maximum(n_visible_bin, 1), np.nan)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 7: \"**Tongue visibility threshold** `likelihood > 0.9`. The DeepLabCut\nlikelihood is extremely bimodal (87 % of frames < 1e-4, 11 % > 0.999); the visible fraction changes\nby < 0.5 % of frames between thresholds of 0.01 and 0.999, so the choice is immaterial (verified in\nStep 10 — 0.1216 at 0.5 vs 0.1168 at 0.9 vs 0.1094 at 0.999). A bin counts as visible if **any**\nframe inside it is visible, because a tongue protrusion lasts only ~50–100 ms and a majority rule\nwould drop genuine short protrusions straddling a bin edge.\" Step 10 Check 3 explains the\ndivergence from the reference's marker handling (\"occluded tongue set to its mean\"): \"the task\ndefines 'not visible' as its own output class, so imputing the mean would destroy exactly the\ndistinction being decoded.\" Step 6 documents the prefix-sum reduction as an efficiency measure.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Four classes. The 40th and 60th percentiles are computed **per session**, over the per-bin mean\ny values of all *visible* bins of all *retained* trials of that session. A bin is then labelled\n0 if its mean y is below the 40th percentile, 2 if above the 60th, 1 in between, and 3 if no frame\nin the bin was visible. `output_values[3] = ['y < 40th pct', 'y 40th-60th pct', 'y > 60th pct',\n'not visible']`. By construction the visible bins split 40/20/40; over the full dataset (where\n74 % of bins have no visible tongue) the four classes are 0.104 / 0.052 / 0.104 / 0.740.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LOW_PCT, TONGUE_HIGH_PCT = 40.0, 60.0\nTONGUE_INVISIBLE = 3\n...\ntongue_class = np.full((n_trials, N_BINS), TONGUE_INVISIBLE, dtype=np.int8)\npercentiles = (np.nan, np.nan)\nif bin_visible.any():\n    visible_values = y_mean[bin_visible]\n    p_low, p_high = np.percentile(visible_values, [TONGUE_LOW_PCT, TONGUE_HIGH_PCT])\n    percentiles = (float(p_low), float(p_high))\n    cls = np.where(y_mean < p_low, 0, np.where(y_mean > p_high, 2, 1))\n    tongue_class[bin_visible] = cls[bin_visible].astype(np.int8)\noutputs[:, 3, :] = tongue_class\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 8: \"**Percentiles for the tongue discretisation** are computed **per\nsession** over the visible per-bin y-values of all retained trials of that session — the population\nthat is actually being labelled — so classes 0/1/2 hold 40 %/20 %/40 % of the visible bins by\nconstruction.\" The fourth class exists because the task's discretisation lists \"3: not visible\".\nStep 10 Check 2 re-derives the classes for every trial × bin of 6 sessions with an independent\nframe-by-frame Python loop and recomputed percentiles: \"PASS, exact equality, percentiles identical\nto 3 decimals\", and the global check \"tongue classes 0/1/2 split the visible bins 0.400 / 0.200 /\n0.400 — PASS\".\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. This is the only genuinely time-varying output. The camera `timestamps` are on the same\nsession-absolute clock as the spikes and go cues, so the frames are binned with `searchsorted`\nagainst exactly the same `edges = go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]` array used for the firing\nrates — bin *k* of the tongue output therefore covers the same interval as bin *k* of the neural\ndata. Trials with no frame at all in the window are dropped (see 1-e); bins with no visible frame\ninside a covered trial become class 3.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = window_edges(go)                     # shared with the neural binning\n...\n_, n_visible_bin, y_sum_bin = segment_sums(\n    raw['tongue_y'], visible, edges, raw['video_t'])\n```\n\n```python\npos = np.searchsorted(sample_times, edges_abs.ravel()).reshape(edges_abs.shape)\n```\n\niii. Step 4 establishes that all NWB streams share one clock and that `dt = 0.0034 s` exactly,\nmatching the reference's marker alignment `times_for_frames = arange(n_frames)*0.0034 − go_time`;\nStep 10 Check 3(c) records the comparison as \"same\". The alignment was checked visually in panel 5\nof the processing figures (\"the raw 300 Hz tongue trace, the per-bin mean of the *visible* frames …\nand the resulting class trace\") and panel 7 (\"class 3 almost everywhere before the go cue and\nlicking structure after it\").\n\n## 9. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Missing data is either excluded (when nothing was recorded) or given an explicit category (when\nthe measurement legitimately has no value):\n\n- **Session never quality-controlled** (`classification`/`anno_name` all NaN, 1 session): no unit\n  matches `== 'good'`, so `good` is empty and the session is rejected with `'no good units'`.\n- **Ephys stops before the behaviour ends** (8 sessions): trials outside the units'\n  `obs_intervals` are dropped, which removed 736 trials and left \"0 all-silent trials\" in the\n  output.\n- **Video stops before the session ends** (3 sessions): trials with no frame in the window are\n  dropped (239 trials); one session then falls below the behavioural criteria and is dropped.\n- **Tongue not tracked in a bin**: that bin gets the explicit class 3 (`'not visible'`).\n- **Trials with no genuine behavioural report** (`auto_water`, `free_water`): dropped.\n- **Bins that fall outside the trial's `[start_time, stop_time]`** (2.9 % on average) necessarily\n  contain no spikes and get rate 0; this is documented, not patched, in\n  `metadata['known_limitation']`.\n- **Session-level failure of any kind**: a worker-level `try/except` records the exception as a\n  rejection reason instead of aborting the run.\n\nii.\n```python\nclassification = np.asarray(units['classification'][:])\ngood = np.flatnonzero(classification == 'good')\n...\nif n_good == 0:\n    reject = 'no good units'\n```\n\n```python\nkeep = raw['recorded'] & (raw['auto_water'] == 0) & (raw['free_water'] == 0)\nno_video = keep & (n_frames_all == 0)\nkeep &= n_frames_all > 0\n```\n\n```python\ntongue_class = np.full((n_trials, N_BINS), TONGUE_INVISIBLE, dtype=np.int8)\n...\ntongue_class[bin_visible] = cls[bin_visible].astype(np.int8)\n```\n\n```python\n'known_limitation': 'The NWB release stores spikes only within each trial\\'s '\n                    '[start_time, stop_time] interval ... so those bins contain no '\n                    'spikes and have a firing rate of 0.',\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 5 enumerates every edge case and its handling, and Step 10 \"Issues Found and\nResolved\" documents that the `obs_intervals` problem was discovered from a processing plot showing\nan empty raster and fixed by adding `recorded_trials()`. The reasoning for the no-video drop is\n\"every bin would otherwise be labelled 'tongue not visible' when the truth is 'not measured'\", and\nfor the tongue class 3 that \"the task defines 'not visible' as its own output class, so imputing\nthe mean would destroy exactly the distinction being decoded.\" Counts of every dropped category are\npreserved per session in `metadata['session_info']`.\n\n## 10-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. Per session, reading the NWB file (the `spike_times` buffer and the ~680 k × 3 tongue array) and\nthe per-unit `searchsorted` spike binning dominate; a session takes 0.5–1.3 s. Across the run, with\n24 worker processes, all 174 files convert in ~15 s and the 9.66 GB pickle write takes ~11 s, for\n25 s total — far below the 15-minute budget in the instructions. The script prints a per-session\nelapsed time and the total, and `--show-processing`/plotting is optional and excluded from the\nnormal path.\n\nii.\n```python\nt0 = time.time()\nwith NWBHDF5IO(path, 'r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n    ...\n    'elapsed': time.time() - t0,\n```\n\n```python\nprint(f'  + {res[\"identifier\"]}: {res[\"neural\"].shape[0]} trials x '\n      f'{res[\"neural\"].shape[1]} units  ({res[\"elapsed\"]:.1f}s)')\n```\n\n```python\nt_write = time.time()\nwith open(args.outfile, 'wb') as f:\n    pickle.dump(data, f, protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)\nprint(f'wrote {size / 1e9:.2f} GB in {time.time() - t_write:.1f} s')\nprint(f'total elapsed {time.time() - t_start:.1f} s')\n```\n\niii. Step 7 \"Run Time Estimates\" tabulates measured times per step and the speed-ups that produced\nthem; Step 7 concludes \"Well under the 15-minute budget, so no further optimisation was needed.\"\n\n## 10-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. Two of the three natural loops were removed. Spike binning keeps one Python iteration **per\nunit** but handles all trials and bins in a single `searchsorted` per unit (the edges of all trials\nare flattened into one call); this loop cannot be collapsed further because `spike_times` is ragged\nand each unit has a different number of spikes. The video reduction has **no** Python loop at all —\nprefix sums over the whole session, indexed by the edge positions, give every (trial, bin) statistic\nin three vectorised operations. The loops that remain and could in principle be vectorised are the\nper-photostim-event loop (one iteration per stim event, ≤ a few hundred per session), the\n`OUTCOME_CODE` / `annotation_to_region` list comprehensions (one per trial / per neuron), and the\nper-trial list splitting in `assemble`; none is a measurable share of runtime.\n\nii.\n```python\n# vectorised over trials and bins; one iteration per unit\nfor i, unit in enumerate(raw['good_units']):\n    counts[i] = bin_spike_times(np.asarray(spike_index[int(unit)]), edges)\n```\n\n```python\n# fully vectorised video reduction\ncum_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(mask)])\ncum_v = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(np.where(mask, values, 0.0))])\nn_masked_bin = cum_n[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_n[pos[:, :-1]]\nmasked_sum = cum_v[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_v[pos[:, :-1]]\n```\n\n```python\n# remaining small loop, one iteration per photostim event\nfor row, on, off in zip(position[in_kept], raw['photostim_start'][in_kept],\n                        raw['photostim_stop'][in_kept]):\n    overlap = (edges[row, :-1] < off) & (edges[row, 1:] > on)\n    photostim[row, overlap] = 1.0\n```\n\niii.
