How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. To **go-cue onset**, using `BehavioralEvents/go_start_times.timestamps` (one per trial,\nasserted). Spike times and event timestamps are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no\nresampling or offset correction is needed: the fixed relative edge grid is added to each trial's\ngo-cue time to give absolute bin edges, and spikes are binned against those directly.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s, signed offset of the window start from the go cue\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s, signed offset of the window end from the go cue\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_WIDTH * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)       # (81,)\n```\n\n```python\ngo = go[trial_idx]\nedges = window_edges(go)          # go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]\n...\ncounts[i] = bin_spike_times(np.asarray(spike_index[int(unit)]), edges)\n```\n\n```python\n'temporal_alignment_event': 'go cue onset (auditory go cue, BehavioralEvents/'\n                            'go_start_times; one per trial)',\n'off_start': OFF_START,\n'off_end': OFF_END,\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 5: \"**Alignment**: go-cue onset (`go_start_times`), one per trial,\nverified in all 174 sessions. Window −2.5 s → +1.5 s, 80 bins of 50 ms.\" Step 10 Check 3(c)\ncompares this with the reference, where \"spike times [are] already go-cue-relative in the `.mat`\nexport\", and concludes \"same\". The alignment was verified visually (panel 3 of the processing\nfigures shows the population PSTH jumping exactly at t = 0 and then splitting by lick direction)\nand numerically (a whole trial re-binned from the raw NWB spike times with `np.histogram`).\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms, non-overlapping, 80 bins spanning [-2.5, +1.5) s relative to the go cue, identical for\nevery trial and every session. The grid is defined once at module level as 81 relative edges and\nreused everywhere; bin *b* is the half-open interval `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))` and bin\ncentres `-2.475 + 0.05b` are used for time-valued inputs. This is a deviation from the reference's\n40 ms-wide / 3.4 ms-stride sliding bins, made because the task prescribes 50 ms bins. There is no\nsecond rebinning step: spikes and video frames are each binned once, directly onto this grid.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5\nOFF_END = 1.5\nBIN_WIDTH = 0.05          # s\nN_BINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_WIDTH))          # 80\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_WIDTH * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)       # (81,)\nBIN_CENTERS = 0.5 * (BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_EDGES[1:])            # (80,)\n```\n\n```python\n'time_bin_size': BIN_WIDTH * 1000.0,\n'bin_centers_s': BIN_CENTERS.astype(np.float32),\n```\n\niii. Step 3 Processing Details: \"reference uses 40 ms width / 3.4 ms stride sliding bins → firing\n**rate** (spikes / bin_width). The present task instead prescribes **50 ms bins**, so I use\nnon-overlapping 50 ms bins over `[-2.5, +1.5)` s (80 bins), rate = count / 0.05 s.\" Step 10 Check 5\nrecords the half-open convention: \"bin *b* is `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))`, half-open, so no\nspike or frame is double counted; verified by the exact re-binning sanity check.\"\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times.timestamps` (the sample-epoch / instruction-tone onsets of\nthe session) together with the trial's go cue. A trial can contain several sample onsets because an\nearly lick replays the sample epoch, so the tone of a trial is defined as the **last**\n`sample_start_times` at or before that trial's go cue. The code asserts that such a tone exists\nand that it lies inside the trial.\n\nii.\n```python\n'sample_start': np.asarray(events['sample_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64),\n```\n\n```python\n# Tone onset = last sample-epoch onset at or before the go cue.  Early licking\n# replays the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several onsets; the\n# most recent one is the tone the animal is acting on.\ntone_idx = np.searchsorted(raw['sample_start'], go, side='right') - 1\nassert np.all(tone_idx >= 0), f\"{raw['identifier']}: go cue before any tone\"\ntone = raw['sample_start'][tone_idx]\nassert np.all(tone >= raw['start_time'][trial_idx] - 1e-9), (\n    f\"{raw['identifier']}: tone onset outside its trial\")\n```\n\niii. Step 4: \"Replays produce extra sample/delay onsets. 'Tone onset' is therefore defined as the\n**last** `sample_start_times` at or before the trial's go cue (always inside the trial: 0\nviolations dataset-wide).\" Step 5 maps it to the reference's `task_sample_time`.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. Because the bins are laid out around the go cue, the value of bin *b* on trial *t* is simply the\nbin centre plus the go-cue-to-tone gap: `BIN_CENTERS[b] + (go[t] - tone[t])`. The result is a\ncontinuous, time-varying `float32` row; it is negative for bins before the tone. Observed range on\nthe full dataset is [-1.525, 11.894] s (the long tail comes from early-lick replays that push the\ntone far back from the go cue).\n\nii.\n```python\ntime_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n...\ninputs = np.stack([time_from_tone, photostim], axis=1)  # (n_trials, 2, 80)\n```\n\n```python\n'seconds elapsed since the onset of the instruction tone (the last sample-epoch '\n'onset at or before the go cue; negative before the tone). Continuous.',\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"input value at bin *b* = `bin_centre_b − (tone_onset − go)` (seconds\nsince the tone)\". Step 9 cross-checks the resulting range against the raw data: \"go − tone: median\n1.85 s, min 0.95, max 10.42\" and notes the converted range [-1.525, 11.894] s is consistent once\nbin centres (±2.475 s) are added. Step 10 Check 2 re-derives 25 random (trial, bin) values straight\nfrom the NWB with `np.allclose(atol=1e-4)`.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is computed on exactly the grid that defines the neural binning — the same 80 bin centres of\nthe same go-cue-anchored window — so bin *k* of the input covers the same interval as bin *k* of\nthe firing rates by construction. No interpolation or separate alignment step exists.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_WIDTH * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)       # (81,)\nBIN_CENTERS = 0.5 * (BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_EDGES[1:])            # (80,)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = window_edges(go)                                     # neural\ntime_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]) # input 0\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 5: \"Bin *b* spans `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))`; the bin centre\n`-2.475 + 0.05b` is used for time-valued inputs.\" The `--show-processing` figure (panel 4) was used\nto confirm the alignment visually: \"the ramp cross[es] zero exactly at the marked true tone onset\".\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Photostimulation* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times.timestamps` and\n`BehavioralEvents/photostim_stop_times.timestamps` — the absolute on/off times of each\nphotostimulation event. The trials-table column `photostim_onset` (a string, `'N/A'` when there was\nno stimulation) is read but used only for the control-trial definition in session curation and as a\ncross-check. The trials table `start_time` is used to assign each stim event to its trial.\n\nii.\n```python\n'photostim_onset_str': np.asarray(trials['photostim_onset'][:]),\n'photostim_start': np.asarray(events['photostim_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64),\n'photostim_stop': np.asarray(events['photostim_stop_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64),\n```\n\niii. Step 1: \"The reference's photostim variable is `[laser_power, stim_type, laser_on_time,\nlaser_off_time]`, with on/off times re-referenced to the go cue. The NWB equivalent is\n`BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times`/`photostim_stop_times` (absolute) plus the trials-table\ncolumns `photostim_onset`/`photostim_power`/`photostim_duration`.\" Step 4 verifies the two are\nconsistent: \"`len(photostim_start_times)` equals the number of trials with\n`photostim_onset != 'N/A'` and they map 1:1 to those trials **in all 174 sessions**\", which\njustifies using the event timestamps (which need no string parsing) as the source.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. A binary (0/1 `float32`) time series, one value per 50 ms bin: a bin is 1 if its half-open\ninterval **overlaps** any `[photostim_start, photostim_stop)` interval. Each stim event is first\nmapped to its trial via `searchsorted` on `start_time`, then to the row of the kept-trial array;\nevents belonging to dropped trials are discarded. Trials and sessions with no stimulation come out\nall-zero.\n\nii.\n```python\nphotostim = np.zeros((n_trials, N_BINS), dtype=np.float32)\nif len(raw['photostim_start']):\n    # A bin [t0, t1) is \"on\" if it intersects any [stim_start, stim_stop).\n    stim_trial = np.searchsorted(raw['start_time'], raw['photostim_start'],\n                                 side='right') - 1\n    position = np.searchsorted(trial_idx, stim_trial)\n    in_kept = (position < n_trials) & (trial_idx[np.clip(position, 0, n_trials - 1)]\n                                       == stim_trial)\n    for row, on, off in zip(position[in_kept], raw['photostim_start'][in_kept],\n                            raw['photostim_stop'][in_kept]):\n        overlap = (edges[row, :-1] < off) & (edges[row, 1:] > on)\n        photostim[row, overlap] = 1.0\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"1 if the bin `[t0,t1)` intersects `[stim_start, stim_stop)`, else 0\",\nmapped to the reference's `task_stimulation[:,2:]`. The task specification requires\n\"Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\", so a per-trial\nflag was rejected in favour of a binary time series. Step 10 Check 5 covers the boundary case:\n\"Photostim offset 1 ms *after* the go cue (34.6 % of stim events) — kept as-is; it affects the\nsingle bin [0, 50 ms) and reflects the real stimulus\", and Step 4 confirms the timing against the\npaper's \"always ended before the Go cue\".\n\n## 4-c. How is the `input` *Photostimulation* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Via the same absolute bin-edge array used for the spikes: `edges` is `go[:, None] +\nBIN_EDGES[None, :]`, and the stim on/off times are absolute session times, so they are compared\nagainst those edges directly. No re-referencing or interpolation is done beyond mapping the event\nto its trial row.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = window_edges(go)               # same array used to bin the spikes\n...\noverlap = (edges[row, :-1] < off) & (edges[row, 1:] > on)\nphotostim[row, overlap] = 1.0\n```\n\niii. Everything in the NWB file is on one session-absolute clock (Step 4), so using the same\n`edges` array guarantees bin-for-bin correspondence with the firing rates. Verified in Step 10\nCheck 2 (\"**input 1**, 100 random (trial, bin) cells — overlap of the bin with any\n`[photostim_start, photostim_stop)` — PASS\") and visually in panel 1/4 of the processing figures,\nwhere the shaded photostim window in the spike raster coincides with the square wave in the input.\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction choice* derived from?\n\ni. The trials table has no choice column, so choice is derived from two columns:\n`trials['trial_instruction']` (`'left'` / `'right'`) and `trials['outcome']`\n(`'hit'` / `'miss'` / `'ignore'`).\n\nii.\n```python\n'instruction': np.asarray(trials['trial_instruction'][:]),\n'outcome': np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:]),\n...\ninstruction = raw['instruction'][trial_idx]\noutcome = raw['outcome'][trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"`trials['trial_instruction']` + `trials['outcome']` →\n`output[0]` = `lick_direction_choice`\", mapped to the reference's `trial_type` × `correctness`\n(`create_4fold_trial_type_mask`). Key Decision 9: \"This is the standard reading of `outcome` in\nthis task and matches the reference's `correctness` semantics (1 correct / 0 error / −1 no\nresponse).\"\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction choice*?\n\ni. Start from the instructed side (`left` → 0, `right` → 1); on a `miss` (error) trial flip it,\nbecause the mouse licked the opposite port; on an `ignore` trial set it to 2 (`no lick`). The\nresult is one integer per trial, written into row 0 of the `(n_trials, 4, 80)` `int8` output array\nand repeated across all 80 bins so that all four outputs share one time-varying array.\n`output_values[0] = ['left', 'right', 'no lick']`. Full-dataset distribution: left 0.447,\nright 0.443, no lick 0.109.\n\nii.\n```python\nCHOICE_LEFT, CHOICE_RIGHT, CHOICE_NOLICK = 0, 1, 2\n...\nchoice = np.where(instruction == 'left', CHOICE_LEFT, CHOICE_RIGHT)\n# An error trial means the mouse licked the port opposite the instruction.\nchoice = np.where(outcome == 'miss', 1 - choice, choice)\nchoice = np.where(outcome == 'ignore', CHOICE_NOLICK, choice)\n...\noutputs = np.empty((n_trials, 4, N_BINS), dtype=np.int8)\noutputs[:, 0, :] = choice[:, None]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 9: \"**Choice on error trials** is the *opposite* of the instruction (the\nmouse licked the wrong port), and `no lick` on `ignore` trials.\" Step 10 Check 2 verifies the\nderivation for every trial of 6 random sessions directly from the NWB, and includes the global\nconsistency check \"choice 'no lick' ⇔ outcome 'ignore' — PASS\".\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?\n\ni. Directly from `trials['outcome']`, which already holds exactly the three strings `'ignore'`,\n`'miss'` and `'hit'`.\n\nii.\n```python\n'outcome': np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:]),\n...\noutcome = raw['outcome'][trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 2 records that `outcome ∈ {hit, miss, ignore}` in the trials table and Step 5 maps it\none-to-one onto the requested output categories; no derivation is needed. The reference analogue is\n`behavior_report` / `correctness` (1 / 0 / −1).\n\n## 6-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?\n\ni. The three strings are mapped through a fixed dictionary to `0` ignore, `1` miss, `2` hit — the\norder given in the task specification — and written into row 1 of the output array, repeated across\nall 80 bins. `output_values[1] = ['ignore', 'miss', 'hit']`. Full-dataset distribution: ignore\n0.109, miss 0.153, hit 0.737.\n\nii.\n```python\nOUTCOME_CODE = {'ignore': 0, 'miss': 1, 'hit': 2}\n...\noutcome_code = np.array([OUTCOME_CODE[o] for o in outcome], dtype=np.int8)\noutputs[:, 1, :] = outcome_code[:, None]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"`trials['outcome']` → `output[1]` = `outcome`; `ignore`→0, `miss`→1,\n`hit`→2\", i.e. the code order of the instructions' \"Outcome (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\". It is\na per-trial label, so it is broadcast across bins like the other per-trial outputs.\n\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Early lick* derived from?\n\ni. Directly from `trials['early_lick']`, which holds `'early'` / `'no early'`.\n\nii.\n```python\n'early_lick': np.asarray(trials['early_lick'][:]),\n...\nearly = raw['early_lick'][trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 2/Step 5: the trials table flags early licking explicitly, so no derivation is needed;\nthe reference analogue is `behavior_early_report`.\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Early lick*?\n\ni. A boolean comparison to `'early'`, cast to `int8` (0 no, 1 yes), written into row 2 of the\noutput array and repeated across all 80 bins. `output_values[2] = ['no', 'yes']`. Full-dataset\ndistribution: no 0.885, yes 0.115 — matching the 0.114 early-lick fraction measured directly on\nthe raw trials tables.\n\nii.\n```python\nearly_code = (early == 'early').astype(np.int8)\n...\noutputs[:, 2, :] = early_code[:, None]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"`trials['early_lick']` → `output[2]`; `no early`→0, `early`→1\". The\nearly lick itself occurs during the sample or delay epoch, i.e. inside the -2.5 s window, but the\nflag is stored per trial, so it is broadcast across bins.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue y-position* derived from?\n\ni. `nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']`, whose\n`data` is `(n_frames, 3)` = (tongue x, tongue y, DeepLabCut likelihood) with matching per-frame\n`timestamps` (dt = 0.0034 s, ≈294 Hz). Column 1 is the y value, column 2 decides visibility; column\n0 is read but unused. The series is present in all 174 sessions.\n\nii.\n```python\ntongue = tracking['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\nout['video_t'] = np.asarray(tongue.timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64)\ntongue_data = np.asarray(tongue.data[:], dtype=np.float64)\nout['tongue_y'] = tongue_data[:, 1]\nout['tongue_likelihood'] = tongue_data[:, 2]\n```\n\niii. Step 2: \"`nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries']` — DeepLabCut tracking, `(n_frames, 3)` =\n`(x, y, likelihood)` with per-frame `timestamps`: `Camera0_side_JawTracking`,\n`Camera0_side_NoseTracking`, `Camera0_side_TongueTracking` (present in **all 174** sessions)\". Step\n5 maps it to the reference's `align_markers_between_lims` / `tongue_y` marker.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Three steps. (1) A frame counts as **visible** if its DeepLabCut likelihood > 0.9. (2) For each\n(trial, bin), the number of visible frames and the sum of their y values are obtained with prefix\nsums over the whole session indexed by the bin edges, giving the per-bin mean y of the *visible*\nframes only; bins with no visible frame get NaN. (3) Those per-bin means are discretised (see 8-c).\nA bin is treated as visible if **any** frame in it is visible.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD = 0.9\n...\ndef segment_sums(values, mask, edges_abs, sample_times):\n    pos = np.searchsorted(sample_times, edges_abs.ravel()).reshape(edges_abs.shape)\n    cum_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(mask)])\n    cum_v = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(np.where(mask, values, 0.0))])\n    n_frames_bin = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n    n_masked_bin = cum_n[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_n[pos[:, :-1]]\n    masked_sum = cum_v[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_v[pos[:, :-1]]\n    return n_frames_bin, n_masked_bin, masked_sum\n```\n\n```python\nvisible = raw['tongue_likelihood'] > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD\n_, n_visible_bin, y_sum_bin = segment_sums(\n    raw['tongue_y'], visible, edges, raw['video_t'])\nbin_visible = n_visible_bin > 0\ny_mean = np.where(bin_visible, y_sum_bin / np.maximum(n_visible_bin, 1), np.nan)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 7: \"**Tongue visibility threshold** `likelihood > 0.9`. The DeepLabCut\nlikelihood is extremely bimodal (87 % of frames < 1e-4, 11 % > 0.999); the visible fraction changes\nby < 0.5 % of frames between thresholds of 0.01 and 0.999, so the choice is immaterial (verified in\nStep 10 — 0.1216 at 0.5 vs 0.1168 at 0.9 vs 0.1094 at 0.999). A bin counts as visible if **any**\nframe inside it is visible, because a tongue protrusion lasts only ~50–100 ms and a majority rule\nwould drop genuine short protrusions straddling a bin edge.\" Step 10 Check 3 explains the\ndivergence from the reference's marker handling (\"occluded tongue set to its mean\"): \"the task\ndefines 'not visible' as its own output class, so imputing the mean would destroy exactly the\ndistinction being decoded.\" Step 6 documents the prefix-sum reduction as an efficiency measure.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Four classes. The 40th and 60th percentiles are computed **per session**, over the per-bin mean\ny values of all *visible* bins of all *retained* trials of that session. A bin is then labelled\n0 if its mean y is below the 40th percentile, 2 if above the 60th, 1 in between, and 3 if no frame\nin the bin was visible. `output_values[3] = ['y < 40th pct', 'y 40th-60th pct', 'y > 60th pct',\n'not visible']`. By construction the visible bins split 40/20/40; over the full dataset (where\n74 % of bins have no visible tongue) the four classes are 0.104 / 0.052 / 0.104 / 0.740.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LOW_PCT, TONGUE_HIGH_PCT = 40.0, 60.0\nTONGUE_INVISIBLE = 3\n...\ntongue_class = np.full((n_trials, N_BINS), TONGUE_INVISIBLE, dtype=np.int8)\npercentiles = (np.nan, np.nan)\nif bin_visible.any():\n    visible_values = y_mean[bin_visible]\n    p_low, p_high = np.percentile(visible_values, [TONGUE_LOW_PCT, TONGUE_HIGH_PCT])\n    percentiles = (float(p_low), float(p_high))\n    cls = np.where(y_mean < p_low, 0, np.where(y_mean > p_high, 2, 1))\n    tongue_class[bin_visible] = cls[bin_visible].astype(np.int8)\noutputs[:, 3, :] = tongue_class\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 8: \"**Percentiles for the tongue discretisation** are computed **per\nsession** over the visible per-bin y-values of all retained trials of that session — the population\nthat is actually being labelled — so classes 0/1/2 hold 40 %/20 %/40 % of the visible bins by\nconstruction.\" The fourth class exists because the task's discretisation lists \"3: not visible\".\nStep 10 Check 2 re-derives the classes for every trial × bin of 6 sessions with an independent\nframe-by-frame Python loop and recomputed percentiles: \"PASS, exact equality, percentiles identical\nto 3 decimals\", and the global check \"tongue classes 0/1/2 split the visible bins 0.400 / 0.200 /\n0.400 — PASS\".\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. This is the only genuinely time-varying output. The camera `timestamps` are on the same\nsession-absolute clock as the spikes and go cues, so the frames are binned with `searchsorted`\nagainst exactly the same `edges = go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]` array used for the firing\nrates — bin *k* of the tongue output therefore covers the same interval as bin *k* of the neural\ndata. Trials with no frame at all in the window are dropped (see 1-e); bins with no visible frame\ninside a covered trial become class 3.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = window_edges(go)                     # shared with the neural binning\n...\n_, n_visible_bin, y_sum_bin = segment_sums(\n    raw['tongue_y'], visible, edges, raw['video_t'])\n```\n\n```python\npos = np.searchsorted(sample_times, edges_abs.ravel()).reshape(edges_abs.shape)\n```\n\niii. Step 4 establishes that all NWB streams share one clock and that `dt = 0.0034 s` exactly,\nmatching the reference's marker alignment `times_for_frames = arange(n_frames)*0.0034 − go_time`;\nStep 10 Check 3(c) records the comparison as \"same\". The alignment was checked visually in panel 5\nof the processing figures (\"the raw 300 Hz tongue trace, the per-bin mean of the *visible* frames …\nand the resulting class trace\") and panel 7 (\"class 3 almost everywhere before the go cue and\nlicking structure after it\").\n\n## 9. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Missing data is either excluded (when nothing was recorded) or given an explicit category (when\nthe measurement legitimately has no value):\n\n- **Session never quality-controlled** (`classification`/`anno_name` all NaN, 1 session): no unit\n  matches `== 'good'`, so `good` is empty and the session is rejected with `'no good units'`.\n- **Ephys stops before the behaviour ends** (8 sessions): trials outside the units'\n  `obs_intervals` are dropped, which removed 736 trials and left \"0 all-silent trials\" in the\n  output.\n- **Video stops before the session ends** (3 sessions): trials with no frame in the window are\n  dropped (239 trials); one session then falls below the behavioural criteria and is dropped.\n- **Tongue not tracked in a bin**: that bin gets the explicit class 3 (`'not visible'`).\n- **Trials with no genuine behavioural report** (`auto_water`, `free_water`): dropped.\n- **Bins that fall outside the trial's `[start_time, stop_time]`** (2.9 % on average) necessarily\n  contain no spikes and get rate 0; For each good unit, the 81 absolute\nbin edges of every kept trial are stacked into one `(n_trials, 81)` array, a single\n`np.searchsorted` over the flattened edges gives the running spike count at each edge, and\ndifferencing adjacent counts gives the spike count per bin. The `(n_good, n_trials, 80)` count\nblock is transposed to `(n_trials, n_good, 80)`, cast to `float32` and divided by 0.05 s. No\nsmoothing, normalisation or baseline subtraction.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef window_edges(go_times):\n    return go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]\n\n\ndef bin_spike_times(spike_times, edges_abs):\n    pos = np.searchsorted(spike_times, edges_abs.ravel()).reshape(edges_abs.shape)\n    return np.diff(pos, axis=1).astype(np.int32)\n```\n\n```python\ncounts = np.empty((n_good, n_trials, N_BINS), dtype=np.int32)\nfor i, unit in enumerate(raw['good_units']):\n    counts[i] = bin_spike_times(np.asarray(spike_index[int(unit)]), edges)\nneural = np.ascontiguousarray(\n    counts.transpose(1, 0, 2).astype(np.float32) / BIN_WIDTH)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 6: \"**Firing rate**, not spike count (reference\n`sliding_histogram(rate=True)`): count / 0.05 s.\" Step 1 records that the reference\n`sliding_histogram` \"returns **firing rate = count / bin_width** when `rate=True`\". Step 10 Check 3\n(d) states the rate convention is kept even though the bin width/stride deviate from the\nreference's 40 ms / 3.4 ms sliding bins, because the task prescribes 50 ms bins. Step 6 documents\nthe `searchsorted` formulation as the deliberate speed-up over a per-(unit × trial × bin) loop:\n\"`np.searchsorted` requires only the *haystack* to be sorted, so the trial windows need not be\nglobally monotone.\"\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Only units with `units['classification'] == 'good'` are kept — the materialised output of the\nregion-specific logistic-regression QC classifier of Chen, Liu et al. (2023). No thresholds are\napplied to any of the 15 individual Kilosort quality metrics, `unit_quality` is not used, and the\nper-unit-per-trial `is_good_trials` column is not used. A session with zero good units is rejected.\nThis retains 69,453 / 272,227 units (25.5 %) over the release and 57,023 units in the 142 kept\nsessions (mean 402/session, range 90–923).\n\nii.\n```python\nclassification = np.asarray(units['classification'][:])\ngood = np.flatnonzero(classification == 'good')\n```\n\n```python\nif n_good == 0:\n    reject = 'no good units'\n```\n\n```python\n'neuron_curation': \"units['classification'] == 'good' (per-region quality-control \"\n                   'classifier of Chen, Liu et al. 2023); all such units carry a CCF '\n                   'annotation.',\n```\n\niii. Step 1 Notes: \"The reference uses `qc_mode='classifier'`, i.e. the per-region\nlogistic-regression classifier … In the NWB release this is materialised as the\n`units['classification']` column (`good` / `unlabelled`), so `classification == 'good'` is the\nexact NWB equivalent of the reference's `goodunits/*.mat` lists. (Confirmed: every `good` unit has\na non-empty CCF annotation `anno_name`…)\" Step 5 Key Decision 2 adds \"No further metric\nthresholds: the 15 quality metrics were already consumed by that classifier, so re-thresholding\nthem would double-filter.\" Validation: 69,453 good units / 25.5 % of clusters against the paper's\n69,943 / 25.9 % (attributed to the dandiset version difference), and nine of the eleven per-region\ncounts in the data paper's Fig. 1E reproduced exactly. Step 3 also records that `is_good_trials`\nis True for 99.98 % of unit×trial pairs, \"so no additional per-trial unit masking is applied —\nsame as the reference.\"\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. To **go-cue onset**, using `BehavioralEvents/go_start_times.timestamps` (one per trial,\nasserted). Spike times and event timestamps are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no\nresampling or offset correction is needed: the fixed relative edge grid is added to each trial's\ngo-cue time to give absolute bin edges, and spikes are binned against those directly.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s, signed offset of the window start from the go cue\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s, signed offset of the window end from the go cue\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_WIDTH * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)       # (81,)\n```\n\n```python\ngo = go[trial_idx]\nedges = window_edges(go)          # go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]\n...\ncounts[i] = bin_spike_times(np.asarray(spike_index[int(unit)]), edges)\n```\n\n```python\n'temporal_alignment_event': 'go cue onset (auditory go cue, BehavioralEvents/'\n                            'go_start_times; one per trial)',\n'off_start': OFF_START,\n'off_end': OFF_END,\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 5: \"**Alignment**: go-cue onset (`go_start_times`), one per trial,\nverified in all 174 sessions. Window −2.5 s → +1.5 s, 80 bins of 50 ms.\" Step 10 Check 3(c)\ncompares this with the reference, where \"spike times [are] already go-cue-relative in the `.mat`\nexport\", and concludes \"same\". The alignment was verified visually (panel 3 of the processing\nfigures shows the population PSTH jumping exactly at t = 0 and then splitting by lick direction)\nand numerically (a whole trial re-binned from the raw NWB spike times with `np.histogram`).\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms, non-overlapping, 80 bins spanning [-2.5, +1.5) s relative to the go cue, identical for\nevery trial and every session. The grid is defined once at module level as 81 relative edges and\nreused everywhere; bin *b* is the half-open interval `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))` and bin\ncentres `-2.475 + 0.05b` are used for time-valued inputs. This is a deviation from the reference's\n40 ms-wide / 3.4 ms-stride sliding bins, made because the task prescribes 50 ms bins. There is no\nsecond rebinning step: spikes and video frames are each binned once, directly onto this grid.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5\nOFF_END = 1.5\nBIN_WIDTH = 0.05          # s\nN_BINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_WIDTH))          # 80\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_WIDTH * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)       # (81,)\nBIN_CENTERS = 0.5 * (BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_EDGES[1:])            # (80,)\n```\n\n```python\n'time_bin_size': BIN_WIDTH * 1000.0,\n'bin_centers_s': BIN_CENTERS.astype(np.float32),\n```\n\niii. Step 3 Processing Details: \"reference uses 40 ms width / 3.4 ms stride sliding bins → firing\n**rate** (spikes / bin_width). The present task instead prescribes **50 ms bins**, so I use\nnon-overlapping 50 ms bins over `[-2.5, +1.5)` s (80 bins), rate = count / 0.05 s.\" Step 10 Check 5\nrecords the half-open convention: \"bin *b* is `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))`, half-open, so no\nspike or frame is double counted; verified by the exact re-binning sanity check.\"\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times.timestamps` (the sample-epoch / instruction-tone onsets of\nthe session) together with the trial's go cue. A trial can contain several sample onsets because an\nearly lick replays the sample epoch, so the tone of a trial is defined as the **last**\n`sample_start_times` at or before that trial's go cue. The code asserts that such a tone exists\nand that it lies inside the trial.\n\nii.\n```python\n'sample_start': np.asarray(events['sample_start_times'].timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64),\n```\n\n```python\n# Tone onset = last sample-epoch onset at or before the go cue. Step 4: \"Replays produce extra sample/delay onsets. 'Tone onset' is therefore defined as the\n**last** `sample_start_times` at or before the trial's go cue (always inside the trial: 0\nviolations dataset-wide).\" Step 5 maps it to the reference's `task_sample_time`.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. Because the bins are laid out around the go cue, the value of bin *b* on trial *t* is simply the\nbin centre plus the go-cue-to-tone gap: `BIN_CENTERS[b] + (go[t] - tone[t])`. The result is a\ncontinuous, time-varying `float32` row; it is negative for bins before the tone. Observed range on\nthe full dataset is [-1.525, 11.894] s (the long tail comes from early-lick replays that push the\ntone far back from the go cue).\n\nii.\n```python\ntime_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n...\ninputs = np.stack([time_from_tone, photostim], axis=1)  # (n_trials, 2, 80)\n```\n\n```python\n'seconds elapsed since the onset of the instruction tone (the last sample-epoch '\n'onset at or before the go cue; negative before the tone). Continuous.',\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"input value at bin *b* = `bin_centre_b − (tone_onset − go)` (seconds\nsince the tone)\". Step 9 cross-checks the resulting range against the raw data: \"go − tone: median\n1.85 s, min 0.95, max 10.42\" and notes the converted range [-1.525, 11.894] s is consistent once\nbin centres (±2.475 s) are added. Step 10 Check 2 re-derives 25 random (trial, bin) values straight\nfrom the NWB with `np.allclose(atol=1e-4)`.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Photostimulation* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times.timestamps` and\n`BehavioralEvents/photostim_stop_times.timestamps` — the absolute on/off times of each\nphotostimulation event. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. A binary (0/1 `float32`) time series, one value per 50 ms bin: a bin is 1 if its half-open\ninterval **overlaps** any `[photostim_start, photostim_stop)` interval. Each stim event is first\nmapped to its trial via `searchsorted` on `start_time`, then to the row of the kept-trial array;\nevents belonging to dropped trials are discarded. Trials and sessions with no stimulation come out\nall-zero.\n\nii.\n```python\nphotostim = np.zeros((n_trials, N_BINS), dtype=np.float32)\nif len(raw['photostim_start']):\n    # A bin [t0, t1) is \"on\" if it intersects any [stim_start, stim_stop).\n    stim_trial = np.searchsorted(raw['start_time'], raw['photostim_start'],\n                                 side='right') - 1\n    position = np.searchsorted(trial_idx, stim_trial)\n    in_kept = (position < n_trials) & (trial_idx[np.clip(position, 0, n_trials - 1)]\n                                       == stim_trial)\n    for row, on, off in zip(position[in_kept], raw['photostim_start'][in_kept],\n                            raw['photostim_stop'][in_kept]):\n        overlap = (edges[row, :-1] < off) & (edges[row, 1:] > on)\n        photostim[row, overlap] = 1.0\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping table: \"1 if the bin `[t0,t1)` intersects `[stim_start, stim_stop)`, else 0\",\nmapped to the reference's `task_stimulation[:,2:]`. Step 10 Check 5 covers the boundary case:\n\"Photostim offset 1 ms *after* the go cue (34.6 % of stim events) — kept as-is; it affects the\nsingle bin [0, 50 ms) and reflects the real stimulus\", and Step 4 confirms the timing against the\npaper's \"always ended before the Go cue\".\n\n## 4-c. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction choice* derived from?\n\ni. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction choice*?\n\ni. Start from the instructed side (`left` → 0, `right` → 1); on a `miss` (error) trial flip it,\nbecause the mouse licked the opposite port; on an `ignore` trial set it to 2 (`no lick`). The\nresult is one integer per trial, written into row 0 of the `(n_trials, 4, 80)` `int8` output array\nand repeated across all 80 bins so that all four outputs share one time-varying array.\n`output_values[0] = ['left', 'right', 'no lick']`. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?\n\ni. Directly from `trials['outcome']`, which already holds exactly the three strings `'ignore'`,\n`'miss'` and `'hit'`.\n\nii.\n```python\n'outcome': np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:]),\n...\noutcome = raw['outcome'][trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. The\nearly lick itself occurs during the sample or delay epoch, i.e. inside the -2.5 s window, but the\nflag is stored per trial, so it is broadcast across bins.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue y-position* derived from?\n\ni. `nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']`, whose\n`data` is `(n_frames, 3)` = (tongue x, tongue y, DeepLabCut likelihood) with matching per-frame\n`timestamps` (dt = 0.0034 s, ≈294 Hz). Column 1 is the y value, column 2 decides visibility; column\n0 is read but unused. The series is present in all 174 sessions.\n\nii.\n```python\ntongue = tracking['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\nout['video_t'] = np.asarray(tongue.timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64)\ntongue_data = np.asarray(tongue.data[:], dtype=np.float64)\nout['tongue_y'] = tongue_data[:, 1]\nout['tongue_likelihood'] = tongue_data[:, 2]\n```\n\niii. Step 2: \"`nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries']` — DeepLabCut tracking, `(n_frames, 3)` =\n`(x, y, likelihood)` with per-frame `timestamps`: `Camera0_side_JawTracking`,\n`Camera0_side_NoseTracking`, `Camera0_side_TongueTracking` (present in **all 174** sessions)\". Step\n5 maps it to the reference's `align_markers_between_lims` / `tongue_y` marker.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Three steps. (1) A frame counts as **visible** if its DeepLabCut likelihood > 0.9. (2) For each\n(trial, bin), the number of visible frames and the sum of their y values are obtained with prefix\nsums over the whole session indexed by the bin edges, giving the per-bin mean y of the *visible*\nframes only; bins with no visible frame get NaN. (3) Those per-bin means are discretised (see 8-c).\nA bin is treated as visible if **any** frame in it is visible.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD = 0.9\n...\ndef segment_sums(values, mask, edges_abs, sample_times):\n    pos = np.searchsorted(sample_times, edges_abs.ravel()).reshape(edges_abs.shape)\n    cum_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(mask)])\n    cum_v = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(np.where(mask, values, 0.0))])\n    n_frames_bin = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n    n_masked_bin = cum_n[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_n[pos[:, :-1]]\n    masked_sum = cum_v[pos[:, 1:]] - cum_v[pos[:, :-1]]\n    return n_frames_bin, n_masked_bin, masked_sum\n```\n\n```python\nvisible = raw['tongue_likelihood'] > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD\n_, n_visible_bin, y_sum_bin = segment_sums(\n    raw['tongue_y'], visible, edges, raw['video_t'])\nbin_visible = n_visible_bin > 0\ny_mean = np.where(bin_visible, y_sum_bin / np.maximum(n_visible_bin, 1), np.nan)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 7: \"**Tongue visibility threshold** `likelihood > 0.9`. The DeepLabCut\nlikelihood is extremely bimodal (87 % of frames < 1e-4, 11 % > 0.999); the visible fraction changes\nby < 0.5 % of frames between thresholds of 0.01 and 0.999, so the choice is immaterial (verified in\nStep 10 — 0.1216 at 0.5 vs 0.1168 at 0.9 vs 0.1094 at 0.999). A bin counts as visible if **any**\nframe inside it is visible, because a tongue protrusion lasts only ~50–100 ms and a majority rule\nwould drop genuine short protrusions straddling a bin edge.\" Step 10 Check 3 explains the\ndivergence from the reference's marker handling (\"occluded tongue set to its mean\"): \"the task\ndefines 'not visible' as its own output class, so imputing the mean would destroy exactly the\ndistinction being decoded.\" Step 6 documents the prefix-sum reduction as an efficiency measure.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Four classes. The 40th and 60th percentiles are computed **per session**, over the per-bin mean\ny values of all *visible* bins of all *retained* trials of that session. A bin is then labelled\n0 if its mean y is below the 40th percentile, 2 if above the 60th, 1 in between, and 3 if no frame\nin the bin was visible. `output_values[3] = ['y < 40th pct', 'y 40th-60th pct', 'y > 60th pct',\n'not visible']`. This is not true of the other trial-phase events: `sample_start_times` and `delay_start_times` can have several entries per trial, because a lick during the sample or delay replays that epoch.\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Trials are filtered only for absence of spike data, in two cases. First, trials outside `units/obs_intervals`: in 8 sessions the ephys recording starts after the behaviour, leaving up to 376 leading trials with no spikes. Second, `free_water` trials, which have no spikes anywhere in the window even though `obs_intervals` covers them. A session is dropped entirely if fewer than 2 trials survive. No behavioural quality filter is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\n# filter behavioral trials with no spike data\noi_off = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].data)\noi_start = np.concatenate([[0], oi_off[:-1]])\nobs = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].target.data)[oi_start[good[0]]:oi_off[good[0]]]\nkeep = np.isin(np.round(trials['start_time'].values, 4), np.round(obs[:, 0], 4))\nassert keep.sum() == len(obs), f'{keep.sum()} matched vs {len(obs)} observed'\n\n# filter no water trials\nkeep &= trials['free_water'].values == 0\nif keep.sum() < 2:\n    return None\ntrials = trials[keep]\ngo = go[keep]\n```\n\niii. `obs_intervals` is the file's own record of which trials were observed, and its start times match `trials.start_time`, which makes the mapping exact. The `free_water` exclusion was found empirically — those trials are covered by `obs_intervals` yet contain no spikes at all — and accounts for 2,449 of the 2,451 all-zero trials remaining after the `obs_intervals` filter.\n\nEarly-lick and no-response (`ignore`) trials are deliberately kept, even though the data paper states \"Early lick trials and no response trials were excluded for analysis\", because both are required decoder outputs here. The 2-trial minimum is the target format's requirement.\n\nTogether these remove 3,510 of the 94,370 trials in the retained sessions (3.7%), leaving 90,860.\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. Neural data is derived from `units/spike_times`, the sorted spike times of each unit in session-absolute seconds. Only units with `classification == 'good'` contribute (see 2-c). The go-cue times (`BehavioralEvents/go_start_times`) are the other input, used to place the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\noffs = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].data)\nallst = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].target.data)\nstarts = np.concatenate([[0], offs[:-1]])\n\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n```\n\niii. `spike_times` is the only neural representation in the file, so firing rates are computed from it directly.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times are converted to per-bin firing rates in Hz. For each good unit, the bin edges for every trial are built as one flat array of absolute times, `np.searchsorted` gives the running spike count at each edge, and differencing adjacent counts gives the spike count per bin. Counts are divided by the bin width to give Hz. No smoothing, normalisation, or baseline subtraction is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    # running spike total at each edge; differencing gives the count per bin\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\nrates /= BIN                                  # counts -> Hz\n```\n\niii. Firing rate is computed from the binned spike count over the 50 ms window defined in the instructions. This also matches the reference code, which calls `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` and returns `binSpikes / bin_width`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Only units with `units/classification == 'good'` are kept. No thresholds are applied to any individual quality metric. A session with no such units is dropped entirely. This retains 69,453 of 272,227 units (25.5%), a median of 390 per session.\n\nii.\n```python\n# ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\ncls = _text(units['classification'])\ngood = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\nif good.size == 0:\n    return None\n```\n\niii. `classification` is the verdict of the spike-sorting quality-control classifier described in `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`.\n\n`units/unit_quality` ('good' / 'multi') is deliberately not used: it is an older label that disagrees on 12.2% of the classifier-good units and is far more permissive.\n\nThe one dropped session (`sub-440958_ses-20190216T162508`) has `classification` and `anno_name` set to NaN for all 1,852 units, i.e. it was never quality-controlled. Excluding it gives 173 sessions and 69,453 good units, against the white paper's 173 sessions and 69,943 units.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Spike times and event times are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no alignment step is needed. The bin edges relative to the go cue are added to each trial's go-cue time to give the absolute time window for that trial, and the spikes are binned against those edges directly.\n\nii.\n```python\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n```\n\niii. Everything in the NWB file is timestamped on one global clock, so aligning to the go cue only requires looking up each trial's go-cue time and taking the window around it. There is no resampling or interpolation, and no per-stream offset to correct.\n\n## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n\ni. Spike times are binned into 80 non-overlapping 50 ms bins spanning -2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue. The bin grid is defined once, as 81 edges relative to the go cue, and reused for every trial and session, so every trial has the same 80 timepoints.\n\nii.\n```python\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. The window and the 50 ms bin width are set by the instructions. Defining the grid once as offsets from the go cue gives a constant 80 timepoints per trial, which the target format requires.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* derived from?\n\ni. From `sample_start_times`, the tone onsets of the session, together with the go cue of each trial. The tone taken for a trial is the **last one** before its go cue.\n\nii. The tone of each trial:\n```python\nsample = np.asarray(bev['sample_start_times'].timestamps)\ntone = sample[np.searchsorted(sample, go, side='left') - 1]\n```\n\niii. An early lick replays the sample epoch, so a trial can carry more than one tone; the last one before the go cue is the one the animal actually used.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *time_from_tone_onset*?\n\ni. The bins sit around the go cue, so the value of a bin is its center plus the gap between the tone and the go cue.\n\nii. The bin center, and the shift that turns them into time from the tone:\n```python\nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n```python\n# bins sit around the go cue, values are seconds since the tone\ntime_from_tone = CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]\n```\n\niii. No additional processing needed other than find the tone onset time.\n\n## 3-c. How is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is how the neural binnning grid is defined.\n\nii. The grid, defined once as offsets from the go cue, and laid on each trial's go cue to bin the spikes:\n```python\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. np.asarray(units['classification'][:])\n    good = np.flatnonzero(classification == 'good')\n    out['recorded'] = recorded_trials(units, good, out['start_time'], out['stop_time'],\n                                      out['identifier'])\n    anno = np.asarray(units['anno_name'][:])[good]\n    electrode_idx = np.asarray(units['electrodes'].target.data[:])[good]\n    electrodes = nwb.electrodes\n    ccf = np.stack([np.asarray(electrodes['x'].data[:]),\n                    np.asarray(electrodes['y'].data[:]),\n                    np.asarray(electrodes['z'].data[:])], axis=1)[electrode_idx]\n    out['good_units'] = good\n    out['anno'] = anno\n    out['ccf'] = ccf\n    return out\n\n\ndef session_performance(raw, keep):\n    \"\"\"Behavioural statistics used for session curation.\n\n    Performance is the fraction of `hit` among control (no photostim), non-early-lick\n    trials with a lick response, following the data paper's definition.\n\n    Args:\n        raw: output of `read_session`.\n        keep: (n_trials,) bool mask of the trials that survive trial curation.\n\n    Returns:\n        (performance, n_correct_left, n_correct_right)\n    \"\"\"\n    control = (raw['photostim_onset_str'] == 'N/A') & (raw['early_lick'] == 'no early') \\\n        & keep\n    hit = raw['outcome'] == 'hit'\n    miss = raw['outcome'] == 'miss'\n    n_hit = int(np.sum(hit & control))\n    n_miss = int(np.sum(miss & control))\n    performance = n_hit / (n_hit + n_miss) if (n_hit + n_miss) else 0.0\n    n_left = int(np.sum(hit & control & (raw['instruction'] == 'left')))\n    n_right = int(np.sum(hit & control & (raw['instruction'] == 'right')))\n    return performance, n_left, n_right\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Per-session conversion\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef convert_session(path, collect_debug=False):\n    \"\"\"Convert one NWB session file.\n\n    Args:\n fails\n        curation.  Keys: 'neural' (n_trials, n_neurons, 80) float32,\n        'input' (n_trials, 2, 80) float32, 'output' (n_trials, 4, 80) int8,\n        plus identifiers and per-neuron metadata.\n    \"\"\"\n    t0 = time.time()\n    with NWBHDF5IO(path, 'r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n        nwb = io.read()\n        raw = read_session(nwb)\n\n        n_good = len(raw['good_units'])\n        go = raw['go']\n        n_trials_all = len(raw['start_time'])\n        assert len(go) == n_trials_all, (\n            f\"{raw['identifier']}: {len(go)} go cues for {n_trials_all} trials\")\n\n        # ---- trial curation -------------------------------------------------------\n        # Keep early-lick / no-response / photostim trials: they are the decoder's\n        # outputs and input.  Drop auto-water and free-water trials (reference\n        # `get_regular_trial_mask`), whose `outcome` is not a behavioural report.\n        # Trials outside the electrophysiological recording carry no spikes at all.\n        not_recorded = ~raw['recorded']\n        keep = raw['recorded'] & (raw['auto_water'] == 0) & (raw['free_water'] == 0)\n\n        # ---- session curation -----------------------------------------------------\n        # The data paper's criteria, evaluated on the trials that actually survive\n        # curation, so that a session whose video or ephys covers only a handful of\n        # trials also fails here (the data paper likewise excluded sessions with video\n        # artifacts).\n        performance, n_left, n_right = session_performance(raw, keep)\n        reject = None\n        if n_good == 0:\n            reject = 'no good units'\n        elif len(trial_idx) < 2:\n            reject = f'only {len(trial_idx)} usable trials'\n        elif performance <= MIN_PERFORMANCE:\n            reject = f'performance {performance:.3f} <= {MIN_PERFORMANCE}'\n        elif n_left < MIN_CORRECT_PER_DIRECTION or n_right < MIN_CORRECT_PER_DIRECTION:\n            reject = f'correct trials L={n_left} R={n_right} < {MIN_CORRECT_PER_DIRECTION}'\n        if reject is not None:\n            return {'identifier': raw['identifier'], 'path': path, 'rejected': reject,\n                    'performance': performance, 'n_good_units': n_good}\n\n        n_trials = len(trial_idx)\n        go = go[trial_idx]\n        edges = window_edges(go)\n\n        # ---- neural ---------------------------------------------------------------\n        units = nwb.units\n        spike_index = units['spike_times']\n        counts = np.empty((n_good, n_trials, N_BINS), dtype=np.int32)\n        for i, unit in enumerate(raw['good_units']):\n            counts[i] = bin_spike_times(np.asarray(spike_index[int(unit)]), edges)\n        neural = np.ascontiguousarray(\n            counts.transpose(1, 0, 2).astype(np.float32) / BIN_WIDTH)\n\n        # ---- inputs ---------------------------------------------------------------\n        # Tone onset = last sample-epoch onset at or before the go cue.  Early licking\n        # replays the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several onsets; the\n        # most recent one is the tone the animal is acting on.\n        tone_idx = np.searchsorted(raw['sample_start'], go, side='right') - 1\n        assert np.all(tone_idx >= 0), f\"{raw['identifier']}: go cue before any tone\"\n        tone = raw['sample_start'][tone_idx]\n        assert np.all(tone >= raw['start_time'][trial_idx] - 1e-9), (\n            f\"{raw['identifier']}: tone onset outside its trial\")\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n\n        photostim = np.zeros((n_trials, N_BINS), dtype=np.float32)\n        if len(raw['photostim_start']):\n# Dataset Conversion Notes\n\n## Overview\n- **Dataset**: DANDI:000363 \"Mesoscale Activity Map Dataset\" (Chen, Nguyen, Li, Svoboda 2023),\n  version 0.230822.0128. Units *must* be quality-filtered. The reference uses\n  `qc_mode='classifier'`, i.e. the per-region logistic-regression classifier described in\n  `methods.txt` and the QC white paper; its output is the list of **\"good\" units**. In the NWB\n  release this is materialised as the `units['classification']` column (`good` / `unlabelled`),\n  so `classification == 'good'` is the exact NWB equivalent of the reference's `goodunits/*.mat`\n  lists. (Confirmed: every `good` unit has a non-empty CCF annotation `anno_name`, and every\n  `unlabelled` unit has an empty one — matching the reference's additional requirement that a unit\n  have both ephys and histology.)\n- Spike times in the reference `.mat` export are **already aligned to the go cue of their trial**;\n  the NWB stores absolute session times plus a go-cue event per trial, so I do the subtraction.\n- Firing rates are counts divided by the bin width (Hz), not raw counts.\n- Marker (video) sampling interval is `dt = 0.0034 s` (≈294 Hz; the paper calls the cameras 300 Hz).\n- The reference's photostim variable is `[laser_power, stim_type(1=left/2=right/6=bilateral ALM),\n  laser_on_time, laser_off_time]`, with on/off times re-referenced to the go cue. `unit_quality` (`good`/`multi` — Kilosort label),\n  **`classification`** (`good`/`unlabelled` — the QC-classifier label) and **`anno_name`**\n  (CCF v3 annotation, non-empty only for `classification == 'good'`).\n- `nwb.electrodes` — per-electrode CCF coordinates `x` (ML), `y` (DV), `z` (AP) in µm.\n  `units['electrodes']` links each unit to exactly one (peak) electrode → per-unit CCF coordinates.\n- `nwb.electrode_groups[*].location` — JSON with the targeted `brain_regions` (e.g. `\"left ALM\"`),\n  stereotaxic coordinates and insertion angles.\n- `nwb.ogen_sites` — `OBIS470_4` (unilateral ALM) and `OBIS470_6` (bilateral ALM), 473 nm.\n\n### Dataset Size (from data files)\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Files / sessions | 174 (173 with ≥1 `good` unit) |\n| The reference `.mat` export stores\n  spike times already relative to the go cue; markers are aligned with\n  `times_for_frames = arange(n_frames)*0.0034 − go_time` (go-cue-relative), over `[-3, 1.5)` s.\n- **Temporal binning**: reference uses 40 ms width / 3.4 ms stride sliding bins → firing **rate**\n  (spikes / bin_width). The present task instead prescribes **50 ms bins**, so I use\n  non-overlapping 50 ms bins over `[-2.5, +1.5)` s (80 bins), rate = count / 0.05 s.\n- **Marker handling** (method paper Methods): outliers found with a 5-sigma velocity threshold and\n  imputed from neighbouring frames; \"when the tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth … we set\n  the tongue position to its mean value\". Here occlusion is an explicit output category instead.\n\n### Curation Steps\n\n**Neuron curation rules**:\n1. Keep only units labelled `good` by the region-specific QC classifier\n   (`units['classification'] == 'good'`); this is the reference's `qc_mode='classifier'` /\n   `goodunits/*.mat` selection and the paper's 69,943-unit set.\n2. Require a CCF annotation (reference drops units with empty `ccf_label`; in the NWB this is\n   automatic — `anno_name` is non-empty for exactly the `good` units).\n3. `is_good_trials` is True for 99.98 % of unit×trial pairs (only 0.1 % of units have any False\n   entry), so no additional per-trial unit masking is applied — same as the reference.\n\n**Trial curation rules** (reference `get_regular_trial_mask`): no early lick, no auto-water,\nno free-water, no no-response, no photostimulation.\n→ *Only the auto-water and free-water exclusions are adopted here*; see Step 5 \"Key Decisions\"\nfor why early-lick / no-response / photostim trials must be **kept** for this decoding task.\n\n**Session curation**: performance > 65 % and ≥ 50 correct lick-left and ≥ 50 correct lick-right\ncontrol trials (data paper), plus ≥ 1 good unit.\n\n### Decoders Trained (accuracies reported in the papers)\n| Decoded variable | Reported accuracy |\n|---|---|\n| Choice, from **video** (embedding), before sample epoch | AUC 0.51 ± 0.06 (n = 106 sessions) |\n| Choice, from **video**, sample+delay epoch | AUC 0.66 ± 0.12 |\n| Choice, from **video**, 2nd half of response epoch | AUC 0.99 ± 0.01 |\n| Choice, from video markers, response epoch | AUC 0.88 ± 0.01 |\n| Choice, from single-neuron delay firing rate | threshold AUC > 0.65 used to call a neuron \"choice-modulated\" |\nNeither paper reports a multi-class accuracy for choice/outcome/early-lick/tongue decoding from\npopulation neural activity, so there is no direct numerical target for this task's decoder; the\nAUC ≈ 0.99 for post-go-cue choice from video is the closest reference point and implies that\nlick direction is near-perfectly recoverable after the go cue.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Discrepancies Found\n| Topic | Code says | Data shows | Papers say | Resolution |\n|-------|-----------|------------|------------|------------|\n| Unit QC | `goodunits/*.mat` lists from region classifiers | `units['classification'] ∈ {good, unlabelled}`; histogram into 80 non-overlapping 50 ms bins spanning `[-2.5, +1.5)` s; divide by 0.05 s → firing rate in Hz | `process_one_area` + `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` |\n| `BehavioralEvents/go_start_times.timestamps` | alignment event (t = 0) | one per trial | `task_cue_time[0,:]` |\n| `BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times.timestamps` | `input[0]` = `time_from_tone_onset_s` | last sample onset ≤ go cue; input value at bin *b* = `bin_centre_b − (tone_onset − go)` (seconds since the tone) | `task_sample_time` |\n| `BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times` / `photostim_stop_times` | `input[1]` = `photostim_on` | 1 if the bin `[t0,t1)` intersects `[stim_start, stim_stop)`, else 0 | `task_stimulation[:,2:]` |\n| `trials['trial_instruction']` + `trials['outcome']` | `output[0]` = `lick_direction_choice` | `ignore` → `no lick` (2); `hit` → instruction; `miss` → opposite of instruction | `trial_type` × `correctness` (`create_4fold_trial_type_mask`) |\n| `trials['outcome']` | `output[1]` = `outcome` | `ignore`→0, `miss`→1, `hit`→2 | `behavior_report` (`correctness`: −1/0/1) |\n| `trials['early_lick']` | `output[2]` = `early_lick` | `no early`→0, `early`→1 | `behavior_early_report` |\n| `BehavioralTimeSeries/Camera0_side_TongueTracking` (`y`, `likelihood`) | `output[3]` = `tongue_y_position` | per bin: frames with `likelihood > 0.9` are \"visible\"; bin value = mean `y` of visible frames; bins with no visible frame → 3; otherwise 0/1/2 by the session's 40th/60th percentile of the visible bin values | `align_markers_between_lims` (`tongue_y`) |\n| `units['anno_name']` + `electrodes[x,y,z]` | `brain_region_idx[session]` | `ccf_regions.annotation_to_region` → one of 14 coarse groups | `helper_get_neuron_id_area` |\n| `nwb.subject.description` (e.g. `SC015`) | `subjects` / `subject_idx` | unique mouse names | mouse name in the `.mat` filename |\n| `nwb.identifier` | `metadata['session_info']` | e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1` | `sess_name` |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Loading**: `pynwb.NWBHDF5IO` only. Trials, events, units and tracking are read through the\n   `pynwb`/`hdmf` API (`nwb.intervals['trials']`, `nwb.acquisition[...]`, `nwb.units`,\n   `nwb.electrodes`). No direct `h5py` access.\n2. **Unit curation** = `classification == 'good'` (the QC-classifier \"good units\" of the reference\n   pipeline, validated against the paper's 69,943 / 25.9 % figures). No further metric thresholds:\n   the 15 quality metrics were already consumed by that classifier, so re-thresholding them would\n   double-filter.\n3. **Session curation**: ≥1 good unit, **and** the data paper's behavioural criteria (control,\n   non-early-lick performance > 65 %; ≥50 correct lick-left and ≥50 correct lick-right control\n   trials). Validated: the 151 surviving sessions have mean performance 83.3 % (range 65.1–97.0 %)\n   vs the paper's 84 % (65–99 %).\n4. **Trial curation**: drop `auto_water` or `free_water` trials (reference `get_regular_trial_mask`;\n   their `outcome` is not a genuine behavioural report — the DataJoint comment for the equivalent\n   field reads \"1: correct **or free water**\"). Drop trials with no video frame in the analysis\n   window (0.8 %), because every bin would otherwise be labelled \"tongue not visible\" when the\n   truth is \"not measured\".\n   **Deliberate deviation from `get_regular_trial_mask`**: early-lick, no-response (`ignore`) and\n   photostimulation trials are **kept**, because the decoder specification requires `early_lick`\n   (no/yes) and `outcome` (ignore/miss/hit) as outputs and photostimulation as an input — removing\n   those trials would leave those variables constant and the task undefined.\n5. **Alignment**: go-cue onset (`go_start_times`), one per trial, verified in all 174 sessions.\n   Window −2.5 s → +1.5 s, 80 bins of 50 ms. Bin *b* spans `[-2.5 + 0.05b, -2.5 + 0.05(b+1))`;\n   the bin centre `-2.475 + 0.05b` is used for time-valued inputs.\n6. **Firing rate**, not spike count (reference `sliding_histogram(rate=True)`): count / 0.05 s.\n   Bins lying outside the trial's `[start_time, stop_time]` interval necessarily contain no spikes\n   and get rate 0; this is a property of the release (see Step 4), and `metadata` records it.\n7. **Tongue visibility threshold** `likelihood > 0.9`. The DeepLabCut likelihood is extremely\n   bimodal (87 % of frames < 1e-4, 11 % > 0.999); the visible fraction changes by < 0.5 % of frames\n   between thresholds of 0.01 and 0.999, so the choice is immaterial (verified in Step 10).\n   A bin counts as visible if **any** frame inside it is visible, because a tongue protrusion lasts\n   only ~50–100 ms and a majority rule would drop genuine short protrusions straddling a bin edge.\n8. **Percentiles for the tongue discretisation** are computed **per session** over the visible\n   per-bin y-values of all retained trials of that session — the population that is actually being\n   labelled — so classes 0/1/2 hold 40 %/20 %/40 % of the visible bins by construction.\n9. **Choice on error trials** is the *opposite* of the instruction (the mouse licked the wrong\n   port), and `no lick` on `ignore` trials. This is the standard reading of `outcome` in this task\n   and matches the reference's `correctness` semantics (1 correct / 0 error / −1 no response).\n10. **Inputs are exactly the two the task specifies**; the go cue is not added as an input because\n    it is at t = 0 in every trial by construction.\n11. **Brain regions**: 14 coarse groups derived from the per-unit CCF annotation (Step 4). Region\n    names carry no hemisphere; the hemisphere of every neuron (from CCF ML vs the reference's\n    5700 µm midline) is stored separately in `metadata['neuron_hemisphere']`.\n\n### Planned 81)` array and\n  a single `np.searchsorted(spike_times, edges.ravel())` per unit yields every bin count by\n  differencing — `np.searchsorted` requires only the *haystack* to be sorted, so the indicator and of the masked y values,\n  indexed by the same edge positions → whole session in three vectorised operations.\n- **Speed-up**: sessions are converted in 24 worker processes (`ProcessPoolExecutor`).\n- **Memory**: each session is returned as `(n_trials, ...)` blocks and split into the per-trial\n  list only in `assemble`, where the block is dropped immediately afterwards; During the *sample* epoch a\nseries of pure tones (3 kHz → lick right, 12 kHz → lick left) instructed the upcoming action;\na 1.2 s *delay* epoch followed in which licking had to be withheld; an auditory **go cue**\nthen opened a 1.5 s *response* epoch in which the mouse licked the left or right port, a\ncorrect lick being rewarded with water. Licking during sample/delay (\"early lick\") replayed\nthe epoch. On ~20 % of randomly interleaved trials, anterolateral motor cortex (ALM) was\nphotoinhibited (473 nm, 40 Hz, 5 mW/hemisphere) for 0.5 s during the delay, always ending at\nor before the go cue.\n\nTwo to five Neuropixels probes recorded extracellular activity brain-wide while a 300 Hz\nside-view camera tracked the tongue, jaw and nose with DeepLabCut.\n\n### Key statistics of the converted data\n| | |\n|---|---|\n| Sessions | 142 |\n| Mice | 28 (2–10 sessions each) |\n| Trials | 73,845 (mean 520 per session, range 206–796) |\n| Neurons (QC \"good\" units) | 57,023 (mean 402 per session, range 90–923) |\n| Time bins per trial | 80 × 50 ms, from −2.5 s to +1.5 s around the go cue |\n| Behavioural performance | 83.8 % correct (range 65.8–98.9 %) |\n| Brain regions | 14 coarse Allen CCF groups (ALM, Orbital, OtherCortex, Olfactory, Hippocampus, CorticalSubplate, Striatum, Pallidum, Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Midbrain, Pons, Medulla, Cerebellum) |\n\n## How to load and use\n\n```python\nimport pickle\nimport numpy as np\n\nwith open('/app/converted_data.pkl', 'rb') as f:\n    data = pickle.load(f)\n\n# firing rates (Hz) of every good unit in session 0, trial 12: (n_neurons, 80)\nrates = data['neural'][0][12]\n\n# the two decoder inputs for that trial: (2, 80)\ntime_since_tone, photostim_on = data['input'][0][12]\n\n# the four decoded variables for that trial: (4, 80), integer class labels\nchoice, outcome, early_lick, tongue_y = data['output'][0][12]\nprint(data['output_values'][0][choice[0]])     # Early licking\n        # replays the sample/delay epoch, so a trial can contain several onsets; the\n        # most recent one is the tone the animal is acting on.\n        tone_idx =  assert np.all(tone >= raw['start_time'][trial_idx] - 1e-9), (\n            f\"{raw['identifier']}: tone onset outside its trial\")\n        time_from_tone = (BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, choice = np.where(outcome == 'miss', 1 - choice, choice)\n        choice = np.where(outcome == 'ignore', CHOICE_NOLICK, choice)\n        outcome_code = np.array([OUTCOME_CODE[o] for o in outcome], np.where(y_mean < p_low, 0, np.where(y_mean > p_high, 2, 1))\n            tongue_class[bin_visible] = cls[bin_visible].astype(np.int8)\n\n        outputs = np.empty((n_trials, 4, N_BINS), The onsets are stored as strings measured from trial start, with `'N/A'` on the trials that were not stimulated, so they have to be converted and re-expressed against the go cue the bins are aligned on.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *photostim*?\n\ni. A bin is 1 where its center falls between the onset and the offset of the stimulation and 0 elsewhere, so the input is a binary time series rather than a per trial flag.\n\nii. The bins the light is on for:\n```python\n# NaN compares False, so non-stim trials stay 0\nphotostim = ((CENTERS[None, :] >= stim_on[:, None])\n             & (CENTERS[None, :] < stim_off[:, None]))\n```\n\niii. A trial without stimulation keeps NaN bounds, and NaN compares false, so all of its bins come out 0 without a separate branch.\n\n## 4-c. How is `input` *photostim* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The onset and offset are expressed relative to the go cue, which is the event the neural bins are aligned on, so they can be compared against the bin center directly.\n\nii. Tracking is present in all 174 sessions and runs at ~294 Hz.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *tongue_y_position*?\n\ni. Four steps. Frames with `likelihood < 0.5` are set to NaN, since the tracker still reports a position when the tongue is not protruding. The surviving values are averaged into 50 ms bins across the whole session, and the 40th and 60th percentiles of *those bin means* give two class edges. Each trial's window is then binned the same way and digitised against those edges, giving classes 0/1/2. Bins containing no visible frame are assigned a fourth class, `3` (`'not visible'`).\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_CONF = 0.5                # tracking likelihood for the tongue to count as visible\nTONGUE_PCT = (40, 60)            # per-session percentiles -> 3 visible classes\nTONGUE_HIDDEN = 3                # no visible tongue frame in the bin\n```\n\n```python\ny[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n\n# bin the whole session on one grid, then take percentiles of the bin means\ngidx = np.floor((t_cam - t_cam[0]) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\nedges = np.nanpercentile(_bin_mean(gidx, y, int(gidx[-1]) + 1), TONGUE_PCT)\n\n# per trial, bin the same way and digitise against those edges\ncls = np.full((len(go), N_BINS), TONGUE_HIDDEN, np.int8)\nlo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\nhi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\nfor i in range(len(go)):\n    b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n    np.clip(b, 0, N_BINS - 1, out=b)\n    m = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\n    ok = ~np.isnan(m)\n    cls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n```\n\niii. The tongue is visible in only ~10% of frames, and when it is retracted the tracker still emits a position, so those frames are discarded rather than averaged in — including them shifts the percentiles and mixes real protrusions with noise. The likelihood value is effectively binary (89% of frames below 0.01, 10.5% at or above 0.99), so the exact threshold does not matter.\n\nPercentiles are taken over the 50 ms bin means rather than raw frames so the edges are defined on the same quantity that gets discretised; taking them over frames instead skews the resulting class balance, because averaging within a bin pulls values toward the center. The 40th/60th split and the per-session scope both follow the instructions. A fourth class is defined for bins with no visible tongue, which is 75% of all bins.\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *tongue_y_position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. This is the one genuinely time-varying output, so it is the only one needing real alignment. The camera timestamps are on the same session-absolute clock as the spikes and the go cues, so each trial's frame range is found by `searchsorted` on the camera timestamps at `go + T_START` and `go + T_STOP`, and frames are assigned to bins by their offset from `go + T_START` — the same go-cue-relative grid used for the firing rates.\n\nii.\n```python\nlo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\nhi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\nfor i in range(len(go)):\n    b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n```\n\niii. The camera timestamps share the global clock with the spikes and events, so no interpolation or offset correction is needed — the same bin grid is applied to both streams, which guarantees bin `k` of the tongue output covers the same interval as bin `k` of the firing rates.\n\nUnlike the spikes, the video is trial-gated: it runs from `trials.start_time` to the trial-end event and is off during the inter-trial interval. On the ~3% of trials where the go cue falls less than 2.5 s after trial start, the leading bins therefore contain no frames at all and fall into the `'not visible'` class.\n\n## 9. Missing data is handled one of two ways depending on what it means. Where nothing was recorded, the session or trial is excluded, since emitting it would fabricate data — a trial with no spikes would otherwise appear as 4 s of 0 Hz across every unit.
